For bronze is potentially a statue in one way, and water is potentially bronze, and air fire, in another. Being potential in this way, could it also be called a power towards what will be, as if the bronze were the power of the statue? Not at all, if the power is taken as the power to make: for the power taken as the power to make could not be called potential. But if the potential is said not only in relation to the actual but also in relation to activity, the potential would be a power too. It is better and clearer, though, to set the potential against the actual, and power against activity. What is potential, then, is something like a substrate for affections, shapes and forms, which it is going to receive and is of a nature to receive, or even hastens to take: some of them for the better, others for the worse, things that ruin it, while each such substrate is also actually something else.
paragraphs.greek: δεῖ τοίνυν τὸ δυνάμει τι ὂν ἄλλο ἤδη τῷ τι καὶ ἄλλο μεθ̓ αὑτὸ δύνασθαι, ἤτοι μένον μετὰ τοῦ ἐκεῖνο ποιεῖν ἢ παρέχον αὑτὸ ἐκείνῳ ὃ δύναται φθαρὲν αὐτό, δυνάμει λέγεσθαι: ἄλλως γὰρ δυνάμει ἀνδριὰς ὁ χαλκός, ἄλλως τὸ ὕδωρ δυνάμει χαλκὸς καὶ ὁ ἀὴρ πῦρ. τοιοῦτον δὴ ὂν τὸ δυνάμει ἆρα καὶ δύναμις λέγοιτο ἂν πρὸς τὸ ἐσόμενον, οἷον ὁ χαλκὸς δύναμις τοῦ ἀνδριάντος; ἤ, εἰ μὲν ἡ δύναμις κατὰ τὸ ποιεῖν λαμβάνοιτο, οὐδαμῶς: οὐ γὰρ ἡ δύναμις ἡ κατὰ τὸ ποιεῖν λαμβανομένη λέγοιτο ἂν δυνάμει. εἰ δὲ τὸ δυνάμει μὴ μόνον πρὸς τὸ ἐνεργείᾳ λέγεται, ἀλλὰ καὶ πρὸς ἐνέργειαν, εἴη ἂν καὶ δύναμις τὸ δυνάμει. βέλτιον δὲ καὶ σαφέστερον τὸ μὲν δυνάμει πρὸς τὸ ἐνεργείᾳ, τὴν δὲ δύναμιν πρὸς ἐνέργειαν λέγειν. τὸ μὲν δὴ δυνάμει τοιοῦτον ὥσπερ ὑποκείμενόν τι πάθεσι καὶ μορφαῖς καὶ εἴδεσιν, ἃ μέλλει δέχεσθαι καὶ πέφυκεν ἢ καὶ σπεύδει ἑλεῖν, καὶ τὰ μὲν ὡς πρὸς τὸ βέλτιον, τὰ δὲ πρὸς τὰ χείρω καὶ λυμαντικὰ αὐτῶν, ὧν ἕκαστον καὶ ἐνεργείᾳ ἐστὶν ἄλλο.

flags.taylor: water (= primalliquid) as potentially bronze
flags.why: The Greek says only "water" (τὸ ὕδωρ); "primal liquid" is MacKenna's gloss.

flags.taylor: the Principle or Abstract in which potentiality
flags.why: The Greek says that if the potential is spoken of in relation to activity, and not only to the actual, it would be a power too; the "Principle or Abstract" in MacKenna's brackets is his.

flags.taylor: in regard to the process of Actualisation
flags.why: The Greek pairs "the potential" with "the actual" (τὸ ἐνεργείᾳ) and "power" with "activity" (ἐνέργεια): two pairs of words, not a process and a principle.

notes: Water as potentially bronze: in Plato's Timaeus (58d-59c) gold, bronze and the other metals are kinds of water, "fusible" water. Air becoming fire is the change of the elements into one another (Timaeus 49b-c).

paragraphs.modern: We must look into matter: whether, being actually something else, it is potentially the things it is shaped into, or actually nothing; and in general whether the other things we call potential, when they take the form and stay themselves, become actual; or whether "actually" will be said of the statue only by setting the actual statue against the potential statue, and not by saying "actually" of that of which "potentially a statue" was said. If so, it is not the potential that becomes actual; rather, from what was potential before, the actual came to be afterwards. For what is actually is the compound of both, not the matter; and the form is what is upon it. This is so when a different substance comes to be, as a statue from bronze: for the statue, as the compound, is a different substance. And with things that do not stay at all it is plain that the potential was altogether different. But when the man who is potentially a grammarian becomes one actually, how is the potential here not the same as the actual? For Socrates potentially wise is the same as Socrates actually wise.
paragraphs.greek: περὶ δὲ τῆς ὕλης σκεπτέον, εἰ ἕτερόν τι οὖσα ἐνεργείᾳ δυνάμει ἐστὶ πρὸς ἃ μορφοῦται, ἢ οὐδὲν ἐνεργείᾳ, καὶ ὅλως καὶ τὰ ἄλλα ἃ λέγομεν δυνάμει λαβόντα τὸ εἶδος καὶ μένοντα αὐτὰ ἐνεργείᾳ γίνεται, ἢ τὸ ἐνεργείᾳ κατὰ τοῦ ἀνδριάντος λεχθήσεται ἀντιτιθεμένου μόνον τοῦ ἐνεργείᾳ ἀνδριάντος πρὸς τὸν δυνάμει ἀνδριάντα, ἀλλ’ οὐ τοῦ ἐνεργείᾳ κατηγορουμένου κατ’ ἐκείνου, καθ̓ οὗ τὸ δυνάμει ἀνδριὰς ἐλέγετο. εἰ δὴ οὕτως, οὐ τὸ δυνάμει γίνεται ἐνεργείᾳ, ἀλλ’ ἐκ τοῦ δυνάμει ὄντος πρότερον ἐγένετο τὸ ἐνεργείᾳ ὕστερον. καὶ γὰρ αὐτὸ τὸ ἐνεργείᾳ ὂν τὸ συναμφότερον, οὐχ ἡ ὕλη: τὸ δὲ εἶδος τὸ ἐπ’ αὐτῇ. καὶ τοῦτο μέν, εἰ ἑτέρα γίγνοιτο οὐσία, οἷον ἐκ χαλκοῦ ἀνδριάς. ἄλλη γὰρ οὐσία ὡς τὸ συναμφότερον ὁ ἀνδριάς: ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν ὅλως οὐ μενόντων φανερόν, ὡς τὸ δυνάμει παντάπασιν ἕτερον ἦν: ἀλλ’ ὅταν ὁ δυνάμει γραμματικὸς ἐνεργείᾳ γένηται, ἐνταῦθα τὸ δυνάμει πῶς οὐ καὶ ἐνεργείᾳ τὸ αὐτό; ὁ γὰρ δυνάμει Σωκράτης ὁ αὐτὸς καὶ ἐνεργείᾳ σοφός.

flags.taylor: a person with a capacity for education becomes in fact educated
flags.why: The Greek is γραμματικός, one who knows letters, a grammarian: Aristotle's stock example of the learner.

notes: The man who is potentially a grammarian, and so a knower in two senses, is Aristotle's (On the Soul II.5, 417a21-b2; Physics VIII.4, 255a33-b5).

paragraphs.modern: Is the man without knowledge, then, a knower, since he was potentially a knower? Or is it the man who is ignorant only by accident who is a knower? For it is not as ignorant that he is potentially a knower: it happened to him to be ignorant, but his soul, fit for it in itself, was what was potential, the very thing by which he is also a knower. So he still keeps the potential, and the man potentially a grammarian keeps it while already being a grammarian. Or nothing prevents it being so in another way too: in the first case only potentially, in this case the power having the form. If, then, the potential is the substrate, and the actual is the compound, the statue, what should we call the form on the bronze? It is not absurd to call the shape and the form the activity by which it is actually and not only potentially: not activity simply, but the activity of this thing. For we might perhaps more properly call something else activity, the one set against the power that brings on activity. For what is potential has its being actual from another; but a power has from itself the activity of what it can do: as a settled state and the activity named after it, courage and acting bravely. So much for that.
paragraphs.greek: ἆρα οὖν καὶ ὁ ἀνεπιστήμων ἐπιστήμων; δυνάμει γὰρ ἦν ἐπιστήμων. ἢ ὁ κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς ἀμαθὴς ἐπιστήμων; οὐ γὰρ ᾗ ἀμαθὴς δυνάμει ἐπιστήμων, ἀλλὰ συμβεβήκει αὐτῷ ἀμαθεῖ εἶναι, ἡ δὲ ψυχὴ καθ̓ ἑαυτὴν ἐπιτηδείως ἔχουσα τὸ δυνάμει ἦν ᾗπερ καὶ ἐπιστήμων. ἔτι οὖν σώζει τὸ δυνάμει καὶ ὁ δυνάμει γραμματικὸς ἤδη γραμματικὸς ὤν. ἢ οὐδὲν κωλύει καὶ ἄλλον τρόπον: ἐκεῖ μὲν δυνάμει μόνον, ἐνταῦθα δὲ τῆς δυνάμεως ἐχούσης τὸ εἶδος. εἰ οὖν ἐστι τὸ μὲν δυνάμει τὸ ὑποκείμενον, τὸ δ’ ἐνεργείᾳ τὸ συναμφότερον, ὁ ἀνδριάς, τὸ εἶδος τὸ ἐπὶ τοῦ χαλκοῦ τί ἂν λέγοιτο; ἢ οὐκ ἄτοπον τὴν ἐνέργειαν, καθ̓ ἣν ἐνεργείᾳ ἐστὶ καὶ οὐ μόνον δυνάμει, τὴν μορφὴν καὶ τὸ εἶδος λέγειν, οὐχ ἁπλῶς ἐνέργειαν, ἀλλὰ τοῦδε ἐνέργειαν: ἐπεὶ καὶ ἄλλην ἐνέργειαν τάχα κυριώτερον ἂν λέγοιμεν, τὴν ἀντίθετον τῇ δυνάμει τῇ ἐπαγούσῃ ἐνέργειαν. τὸ μὲν γὰρ δυνάμει τὸ ἐνεργείᾳ ἔχει παῤ ἄλλου, τῇ δὲ δυνάμει ὃ δύναται παῤ αὐτῆς ἡ ἐνέργεια: οἷον ἕξις καὶ ἡ κατ’ αὐτὴν λεγομένη ἐνέργεια, ἀνδρεία καὶ τὸ ἀνδρίζεσθαι. ταῦτα μὲν μὲν οὖν οὕτως.

flags.taylor: but by virtue of Actuality (the abstract)
flags.why: The Greek says the power has the activity "from itself" (παρ’ αὐτῆς): it does not act by virtue of an abstract Actuality.

flags.taylor: between a temperament and its expression in act
flags.why: The Greek is ἕξις, a settled state, Aristotle's word for the state a virtue is, not a temperament.

notes: A settled state (ἕξις) and its activity: so Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.1 (1103a31-b2), "by doing brave acts we become brave".

paragraphs.modern: Now we must say why all this was said first: how "actually" is said in the intelligibles, and whether each and all there are only actual, or each is also activity, and whether the potential is there too. If there is no matter there in which the potential is, and nothing there is going to be what it is not already, nor does anything there change into something else, or, staying, beget something other, or, standing out of itself, give way to another to be in its place, then the potential would not be there, where all things are really, things that have eternity and not time. If, then, someone asked those who set matter in the intelligibles too whether there is not the potential there as well, after the matter there (for even if matter is there in another way, still in each thing there will be one part as matter, one as form, and the compound of both), what will they say? That what is as matter there is form too; since soul, being a form, would also be matter in relation to another. Is it not, then, potentially that other? No: for the form was its own, and does not come later, and is not separated except in thought; and so it has matter in that it is thought of as double, but both are one nature: as Aristotle too says that the fifth body is without matter.
paragraphs.greek: οὗ δ’ ἕνεκα ταῦτα προείρηται, νῦν λεκτέον, ἐν τοῖς νοητοῖς πῶς ποτε τὸ ἐνεργείᾳ λέγεται καὶ εἰ ἐνεργείᾳ μόνον ἢ καὶ ἐνέργεια ἕκαστον καὶ πάντα καὶ εἰ τὸ δυνάμει κἀκεῖ. εἰ δὲ μήτε ὕλη ἐκεῖ ἐν ᾗ τὸ δυνάμει, μήτε τι μέλλει τῶν ἐκεῖ, ὃ μὴ ἤδη ἔστι, μηδέ τι μεταβάλλον εἰς ἄλλο ἢ μένον ἕτερόν τι γεννᾷ ἢ ἐξιστάμενον ἑαυτοῦ ἔδωκεν ἄλλῳ ἀνθ̓ αὑτοῦ εἶναι, οὐκ ἂν εἴη ἐκεῖ τὸ δυνάμει, ἐν ᾧ ἐστι πάντα ὄντως, τῶν ὄντων καὶ αἰῶνα, οὐ χρόνον ἐχόντων. εἴ τις οὖν καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν νοητῶν τοὺς τιθεμένους κἀκεῖ ὕλην ἔροιτο, εἰ μὴ κἀκεῖ τὸ δυνάμει κατὰ τὴν ὕλην τὴν ἐκεῖ — καὶ γὰρ εἰ ἄλλον τρόπον ἡ ὕλη, ἀλλ’ ἔσται ἐφ̓ ἑκάστου τὸ μὲν ὡς ὕλη, τὸ δὲ ὡς εἶδος, τὸ δὲ συναμφότερον — τί ἐροῦσιν; ἢ καὶ τὸ ὡς ὕλη ἐκεῖ εἶδός ἐστιν, ἐπεὶ καὶ ἡ ψυχὴ εἶδος ὂν πρὸς ἕτερον ἂν εἴη ὕλη. οὐκοῦν πρὸς ἐκεῖνο καὶ δυνάμει; ἢ οὔ: εἶδος γὰρ ἦν αὐτῆς καὶ οὐκ εἰς ὕστερον δὲ τὸ εἶδος καὶ οὐ χωρίζεται δὲ ἀλλ’ ἢ λόγῳ, καὶ οὕτως ὕλην ἔχον, ὡς διπλοῦν νοούμενον, ἄμφω δὲ μία φύσις: οἷον καὶ Ἀριστοτέλης φησὶ τὸ πέμπτον σῶμα ἄυλον εἶναι.

flags.taylor: who (with us) assert Matter in the Intellectual Realm
flags.why: "With us" is MacKenna's; it is true to Plotinus, who set out an intelligible matter in II.4 (chapters 2-5), but the Greek says only "those who set matter there too".

notes: The fifth body is Aristotle's heavenly body (On the Heavens I.2-3); Aristotle allows it matter only for movement in place, not for coming to be (Metaphysics VIII.4, 1044b7-8; XII.2, 1069b24-26).

paragraphs.modern: But what shall we say about soul? It is potentially a living being, when it is not yet one but is going to be; and potentially musical, and all the other things it becomes, not being them always: so the potential is in the intelligibles too. Or rather it is not potentially these things: soul is the power of them. How, then, is the actual there? Is it as the statue, the compound, is actual, because each thing has received its form? Or because each is a form, and complete as what it is. For intellect does not go from a power of being able to think to the activity of thinking; for then it would need another, prior to it, which did not come from a power; the whole is in it. For what is potential wants something else to come upon it and bring it into activity, so that it may become something actually; but what has from itself what is always so, that would be actual. All the first things, then, are actual: for they have what they must have, from themselves and always. And so is soul, the soul that is not in matter but in the intelligible; and the other soul too, the one in matter, is actual, the soul of growth, for instance: for this one too is actually what it is.
paragraphs.greek: περὶ δὲ ψυχῆς πῶς ἐροῦμεν; δυνάμει γὰρ ζῷον, ὅταν μήπω, μέλλῃ δέ, καὶ μουσικὴ δυνάμει καὶ τὰ ἄλλα ὅσα γίνεται οὐκ ἀεὶ οὖσα: ὥστε καὶ ἐν νοητοῖς τὸ δυνάμει. ἢ οὐ δυνάμει ταῦτα, ἀλλὰ δύναμις ἡ ψυχὴ τούτων. τὸ δὲ ἐνεργείᾳ πῶς ἐκεῖ; ἆρα ὡς ὁ ἀνδριὰς τὸ συναμφότερον ἐνεργείᾳ, ὅτι τὸ εἶδος ἕκαστον ἀπείληφεν; ἢ ὅτι εἶδος ἕκαστον καὶ τέλειον ὃ ἔστι. νοῦς γὰρ οὐκ ἐκ δυνάμεως τῆς κατὰ τὸ οἷόν τε νοεῖν εἰς ἐνέργειαν τοῦ νοεῖν — ἄλλου γὰρ ἂν προτέρου τοῦ οὐκ ἐκ δυνάμεως δέοιτο — ἀλλ’ ἐν αὐτῷ τὸ πᾶν. τὸ γὰρ δυνάμει βούλεται ἑτέρου ἐπελθόντος εἰς ἐνέργειαν ἄγεσθαι, ἵνα ἐνεργείᾳ γίγνηταί τι, ὃ δ’ αὐτὸ παῤ αὑτοῦ τὸ ἀεὶ οὕτως ἔχει, τοῦτο ἐνεργείᾳ ἂν εἴη. πάντα οὖν τὰ πρῶτα ἐνεργείᾳ: ἔχει γὰρ ἃ δεῖ ἔχειν καὶ παῤ αὐτῶν καὶ ἀεί: καὶ ψυχὴ δὴ οὕτως ἡ μὴ ἐν ὕλῃ, ἀλλ’ ἐν τῷ νοητῷ. καὶ ἡ ἐν ὕλῃ δὲ ἄλλη ἐνεργείᾳ: οἷον ἡ φυτική: ἐνεργείᾳ γὰρ καὶ αὕτη ὃ ἔστιν.

flags.taylor: the Form-Idea has mastered each separate constituent
flags.why: The Greek asks whether it is actual "because each has received its form" (ὅτι τὸ εἶδος ἕκαστον ἀπείληφεν); "mastered" is MacKenna's.

flags.taylor: (and not, like material things, merely in image)
flags.why: MacKenna's words in brackets are his; the Greek says only that the soul of growth "too is actually what it is".

paragraphs.modern: But if all are actual, are all of them in this way also activity? Or how? If that nature is rightly said to be sleepless, and life, and the best life, the most beautiful activities would be there. All, then, are both actual and activity, all are lives, and the place there is a place of life, and truly the principle and spring of soul and intellect.
paragraphs.greek: ἀλλ’ ἐνεργείᾳ μὲν πάντα, καὶ οὕτως ἐνέργεια τὰ πάντα; ἢ πῶς; εἰ δὴ καλῶς εἴρηται ἐκείνη ἡ φύσις ἄγρυπνος εἶναι καὶ ζωὴ καὶ ζωὴ ἀρίστη, αἱ κάλλισται ἂν εἶεν ἐκεῖ ἐνέργειαι. καὶ ἐνεργείᾳ ἄρα καὶ ἐνέργεια τὰ πάντα καὶ ζωαὶ τὰ πάντα καὶ ὁ τόπος ὁ ἐκεῖ τόπος ἐστὶ ζωῆς καὶ ἀρχὴ καὶ πηγὴ ἀληθῶς ψυχῆς τε καὶ νοῦ.
notes: "Sleepless" and "the best life" are said of Aristotle's god, whose life is "best and eternal" (Metaphysics XII.7, 1072b26-30) and who, if it thought nothing, would be like one asleep (XII.9, 1074b17-18). The "spring" (πηγή) of soul echoes Plato's Phaedrus (245c), where soul is "the spring and principle of motion".

paragraphs.modern: All the other things, then, that are something potentially, also have being actually something else, which, already being, is said to be potentially in relation to another. But what of what is called matter, which we say is potentially all the beings: how can it be said to be actually any of the beings? Otherwise not all the beings would be potentially in it. If, then, it is none of the beings, it must necessarily not be a being itself. How, then, could it be actually anything, being none of the beings? Still, it would be none of these beings that come to be upon it; but nothing prevents it being something else, if indeed not all the beings are upon matter. But if it is none of the things upon it, and these are beings, it would be non-being. Nor indeed, imagined as something formless, would it be a form: so it could not be counted among those either. So in this way too it will be non-being. Being non-being on both counts, then, it will be non-being all the more. If it has fled the nature of what truly is, and cannot reach even the things falsely said to be, because it is not even a phantom of a forming principle as they are, in what kind of being could it be caught? And if in none, what could it be actually?
paragraphs.greek: τὰ μὲν οὖν ἄλλα πάντα, ὅσα δυνάμει τί ἐστιν, ἔχει καὶ τὸ ἐνεργείᾳ εἶναι ἄλλο τι, ὃ ἤδη ὂν πρὸς ἄλλο δυνάμει εἶναι λέγεται: περὶ δὲ τῆς λεγομένης εἶναι ὕλης, ἣν πάντα δυνάμει λέγομεν τὰ ὄντα, πῶς ἔστιν εἰπεῖν ἐνεργείᾳ τι τῶν ὄντων εἶναι; ἢ γὰρ οὐ πάντα τὰ ὄντα δυνάμει ἂν εἴη. εἰ οὖν μηδὲν τῶν ὄντων, ἀνάγκη μηδ’ ὂν αὐτὴν εἶναι. πῶς οὖν ἂν ἐνεργείᾳ τι εἴη μηδὲν τῶν ὄντων οὖσα; ἀλλ’ οὐδὲν τῶν ὄντων ἂν εἴη τούτων, ἃ γίνεται ἐπ’ αὐτῇ, ἄλλο δέ τι οὐδὲν κωλύει εἶναι, εἴπερ μηδὲ πάντα τὰ ὄντα ἐπὶ τῇ ὕλῃ. εἰ μὲν δὴ οὐδέν ἐστι τούτων τῶν ἐπ’ αὐτῇ, ταῦτα δὲ ὄντα, μὴ ὂν ἂν εἴη. οὐ μὲν δὴ ἀνείδεόν τι φανταζομένη εἶδος ἂν εἴη; οὐ τοίνυν οὐδ’ ἐν ἐκείνοις ἂν ἀριθμηθείη. μὴ ὂν ἄρα καὶ ταύτῃ ἔσται. ἐπ’ ἄμφω ἄρα μὴ ὂν οὖσα καὶ πλειόνως μὴ ὂν ἔσται. εἰ δὴ πέφευγε μὲν τὴν τῶν ὡς ἀληθῶς ὄντων φύσιν, οὐ δύναται δὲ ἐφικέσθαι οὐδὲ τῶν ψευδῶς λεγομένων εἶναι, ὅτι μηδὲ ἴνδαλμα λόγου ἐστὶν ὡς ταῦτα, ἐν τίνι τῷ εἶναι ἂν ἁλοίη; εἰ δὲ ἐν μηδενὶ τῷ εἶναι, τί ἂν ἐνεργείᾳ εἴη;

flags.taylor: this potentiality of the future mode of being is an existing mode
flags.why: The Greek says the thing that is potential is already actually something else, and is said to be potentially in relation to another; it says nothing of a "future mode of being".

flags.taylor: it is not even a phantasm of Reason
flags.why: The Greek is ἴνδαλμα λόγου, a phantom of a forming principle: the bodies that are "falsely said to be" are images of forming principles, and matter is not even that.

notes: "What truly is" and what is falsely said to be: Plato's Timaeus (27d-28a, 52a-c) sets what always is against what comes to be and never is, and makes the receptacle a third kind, grasped "by a bastard reasoning".

paragraphs.modern: How, then, shall we speak of it? How is it the matter of the beings? Because it is potentially. Then, because it is potentially, is it already what it is going to be? No: its being is only the promise of what is going to be; its being, as it were, is put off to what will be. What is potential, then, is not something, but potentially all things; being nothing by itself, but being what it is, matter, it is not actually either. For if it is actually something, that which it is actually will not be matter; it will not be matter in every way, but only as the bronze is. It would be non-being, then, not as different from being, as motion is: for motion rides upon being, coming as it were from it and being in it; but matter is as if cast out and wholly separated, unable to change itself, but always as it was from the beginning; and it was non-being. It was not actually anything from the beginning, standing away from all the beings, nor did it become anything: it has not even been able to take a colour from the things it wished to put on; but staying, being potentially towards something else, towards what came next, it appeared when those beings had already come to an end, and, caught by the things that came to be after it, it settled as the last of these too.
paragraphs.greek: πῶς οὖν λέγωμεν περὶ αὐτῆς; πῶς δὲ τῶν ὄντων ὕλη; ἢ ὅτι δυνάμει. οὔκουν, ὅτι δυνάμει, ἤδη ἔστι καθὸ μέλλει, ἀλλὰ τὸ εἶναι αὐτῇ μόνον τὸ μέλλον ἐπαγγελλόμενον: οἷον τὸ εἶναι αὐτῇ εἰς ἐκεῖνο ἀναβάλλεται, ὃ ἔσται. τὸ τοίνυν δυνάμει οὔ τι, ἀλλὰ δυνάμει πάντα: μηδὲν δὲ ὂν καθ̓ αὑτό, ἀλλ’ ὃ ἔστιν ὕλη ὄν, οὐδὲ ἐνεργείᾳ ἐστίν. εἰ γὰρ ἔστι τι ἐνεργείᾳ, ἐκεῖνο, ὃ ἔστιν ἐνεργείᾳ, οὐχ ὕλη ἔσται: οὐ πάντη οὖν ὕλη, ἀλλὰ οἷον ὁ χαλκός. εἴη ἂν οὖν τὸ μὴ ὄν, οὐχ ὡς ἕτερον τοῦ ὄντος, οἷον κίνησις: αὕτη γὰρ καὶ ἐποχεῖται τῷ ὄντι οἷον ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐν αὐτῷ οὖσα, ἡ δέ ἐστιν οἷον ἐκριφεῖσα καὶ πάντη χωρισθεῖσα καὶ μεταβάλλειν ἑαυτὴν οὐ δυναμένη, ἀλλ’ ὅπερ ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἦν: μὴ ὂν δὲ ἦν: οὕτως ἀεὶ ἔχουσα. οὔτε δὲ ἦν ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἐνεργείᾳ τι ἀποστᾶσα πάντων τῶν ὄντων οὔτε ἐγένετο: ἃ γὰρ ὑποδῦναι ἠθέλησεν, οὐδὲ χρωσθῆναι ἀπ’ αὐτῶν δεδύνηται, ἀλλὰ μένουσα πρὸς ἄλλο δυνάμει οὖσα πρὸς τὰ ἐφεξῆς, τῶν δ’ ὄντων ἤδη παυσαμένων ἐκείνων φανεῖσα ὑπό τε τῶν μετ’ αὐτὴν γενομένων καταληφθεῖσα ἔσχατον καὶ τούτων κατέστη.

flags.taylor: annex for itself even a visible outline
flags.why: The Greek says it could not even "be coloured" (χρωσθῆναι) by the things it wished to slip into: a colour, not an outline.

flags.taylor: it is remoter (from Real-Being) even than they
flags.why: The Greek says that, caught by the things that came to be after it, it "settled as the last of these too" (ἔσχατον καὶ τούτων κατέστη): last in the order, not further from real being.

notes: Non-being as "the different" from being, and motion as different from being and yet partaking in it, are the Eleatic Stranger's in Plato's Sophist (255e-256d, 257b, 258b).

paragraphs.modern: Caught by both, then, it would be actually neither, but is left to be only potentially, something weak and dim, an image unable to be shaped. It is actually, then, an image; it is actually, then, a falsehood. And this is the same as being truly a falsehood, and this is really non-being. If, then, it is actually non-being, it is non-being more, and so really non-being. So it is far from being actually any of the beings, since its truth lies in non-being. If, then, it must be, it must not be actually, so that, having stepped out of true being, it may have its being in non-being; since, with things that are falsely, if you take away their falsehood, you take away whatever being they had; and if you bring activity into things that have their being and their substance in being potential, you have destroyed the cause of their existence, because their being was in potency. If, then, we must keep matter indestructible, we must keep it as matter: so we must say, it seems, that it is only potentially, so that it may be what it is; or else these arguments must be refuted.
paragraphs.greek: ὑπ’ ἀμφοτέρων οὖν καταληφθεῖσα ἐνεργείᾳ μὲν οὐδετέρων ἂν εἴη, δυνάμει δὲ μόνον ἐγκαταλέλειπται εἶναι ἀσθενές τι καὶ ἀμυδρὸν εἴδωλον μορφοῦσθαι μὴ δυνάμενον. οὐκοῦν ἐνεργείᾳ εἴδωλον: οὐκοῦν ἐνεργείᾳ ψεῦδος. τοῦτο δὲ ταὐτὸν τῷ ἀληθινῶς ψεῦδος: τοῦτο δὲ ὄντως μὴ ὄν. εἰ οὖν ἐνεργείᾳ μὴ ὄν, μᾶλλον μὴ ὄν, καὶ ὄντως ἄρα μὴ ὄν. πολλοῦ ἄρα δεῖ αὐτῷ ἐνεργείᾳ τι τῶν ὄντων εἶναι τὸ ἀληθὲς ἔχοντι ἐν τῷ μὴ ὄντι. εἴπερ ἄρα δεῖ αὐτὸ εἶναι, δεῖ αὐτὸ ἐνεργείᾳ μὴ εἶναι, ἵνα ἐκβεβηκὸς τοῦ ἀληθῶς εἶναι ἐν τῷ μὴ εἶναι ἔχῃ τὸ εἶναι, ἐπείπερ τοῖς ψευδῶς οὖσιν, ἐὰν ἀφέλῃς τὸ ψεῦδος αὐτῶν, ἀφεῖλες αὐτῶν ἥντινα εἶχον οὐσίαν, καὶ τοῖς δυνάμει τὸ εἶναι καὶ τὴν οὐσίαν ἔχουσιν εἰσαγαγὼν τὴν ἐνέργειαν ἀπολώλεκας τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτῶν τὴν αἰτίαν, ὅτι τὸ εἶναι αὐτοῖς ἐν δυνάμει ἦν. εἴπερ ἄρα δεῖ ἀνώλεθρον τὴν ὕλην τηρεῖν, ὕλην αὐτὴν δεῖ τηρεῖν: δεῖ ἄρα δυνάμει, ὡς ἔοικεν,εἶναι λέγειν μόνον, ἵνα ᾖ ὃ ἔστιν, ἢ τούτους τοὺς λόγους ἐξελεγκτέον.

flags.taylor: kept as the unchanging substratum
flags.why: The Greek is ἀνώλεθρον, "indestructible": matter must not perish, which it would if it became actual.

notes: Matter as a weak and dim image, truly false, is Plotinus' account in III.6 (chapter 7), where it is a "phantom" (φάντασμα) that holds nothing and promises everything.

paragraphs.modern: Is being different from substance? Is being stripped of the others, while substance is being together with the others, motion, rest, sameness and difference, and these are its elements? The whole, then, is substance, and of those each is being, or motion, or something else. Motion, then, is a being by accident: is it, then, a substance by accident? Or does it complete substance? Or is it too a substance, and all the things there are substance? Why not here too, then? Because there all are one, but here, the images being divided, one is one thing and another another; as in the seed all things are together, and each is all, and hand is not apart and head apart, while here they are separated from each other: for they are images, and not true.
paragraphs.greek: Ἆρα τὸ ὂν καὶ ἡ οὐσία ἕτερον. καὶ τὸ μὲν ὂν ἀπηρημωμένον τῶν ἄλλων, ἡ δὲ οὐσία τὸ ὂν μετὰ τῶν ἄλλων, κινήσεως, στάσεως, ταὐτοῦ, ἑτέρου, καὶ στοιχεῖα ταῦτα ἐκείνης; τὸ οὖν ὅλον οὐσία, ἕκαστον δὲ ἐκείνων τὸ μὲν ὄν, τὸ δὲ κίνησις, τὸ δὲ ἄλλο τι. κίνησις μὲν οὖν κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς ὄν: οὐσία δὴ ἄρα κατὰ συμβεβηκός: ἢ συμπληρωτικὸν οὐσίας; ἢ καὶ αὐτὴ οὐσία καὶ τὰ ἐκεῖ πάντα οὐσία. πῶς οὖν οὐ καὶ ἐνταῦθα; ἢ ἐκεῖ, ὅτι ἓν πάντα, ἐνθάδε δὲ διαληφθέντων τῶν εἰδώλων τὸ μὲν ἄλλο, τὸ δὲ ἄλλο: ὥσπερ ἐν μὲν τῷ σπέρματι ὁμοῦ πάντα καὶ ἕκαστον πάντα καὶ οὐ χεὶρ χωρὶς καὶ χωρὶς κεφαλή, ἐνθάδε δὲ χωρίζεται ἀλλήλων: εἴδωλα γὰρ καὶ οὐκ ἀληθῆ.

flags.taylor: envisage Being as the substance stripped of all else
flags.why: The Greek says only "being stripped of the others" (τὸ μὲν ὂν ἀπηρημωμένον τῶν ἄλλων). MacKenna's "Reality" in this treatise stands for οὐσία, which the modern version calls substance.

notes: Being, motion, rest, sameness and difference are the five greatest kinds of Plato's Sophist (254b-255e); Plotinus takes them as the kinds of the intelligible world in VI.2 (chapters 7-8). The seed in which all the parts are together is the Stoics' "seminal principle"; Plotinus uses it again in III.2.2 and V.9.6.

paragraphs.modern: Shall we say, then, that the qualities there are differences of substance, about substance or about being, differences that make substances different from one another, and substances on the whole? That is not absurd; but there is the question of the qualities here, some of which are differences of substances, as two-footed and four-footed, while others, not being differences, are called qualities for that very reason. And yet the same thing becomes a difference when it completes a substance, and is not a difference in something else, where it does not complete the substance but is an accident: as white completes a swan or white lead, but is an accident in you. Or rather the white in the forming principle completes it and is not a quality, while the white on the surface is a quality. Or we must divide quality: one kind belongs to the substance, being something proper to it; the other is only quality, by which a substance is qualified, the quality making no change into the substance or out of it, but, the substance being already there and completed, making a disposition from outside, an addition after the substance of the thing, whether it comes to be about a soul or about a body.
paragraphs.greek: τὰς οὖν ποιότητας ἐκεῖ φήσομεν οὐσίας διαφορὰς περὶ οὐσίαν οὔσας ἢ περὶ ὄν, διαφορὰς δὲ ποιούσας ἑτέρας οὐσίας πρὸς ἀλλήλας καὶ ὅλως οὐσίας; ἢ οὐκ ἄτοπον, ἀλλὰ περὶ τῶν τῇδε ποιοτήτων, ὧν αἱ μὲν διαφοραὶ οὐσιῶν, ὡς τὸ δίπουν καὶ τὸ τετράπουν, αἱ δὲ οὐ διαφοραὶ οὖσαι αὐτὸ τοῦτο μόνον ποιότητες λέγονται. καίτοι τὸ αὐτὸ καὶ διαφορὰ γίνεται συμπληροῦσα καὶ οὐ διαφορὰ ἐν ἄλλῳ οὐ συμπληροῦσα τὴν οὐσίαν, σημβεβηκὸς δέ: οἷον τὸ λευκὸν ἐν μὲν κύκνῳ ἢ ψιμμυθίῳ συμπληροῦν, ἐν δὲ σοὶ συμβεβηκός. ἢ τὸ λευκὸν τὸ μὲν ἐν τῷ λόγῳ συμπληροῦν καὶ οὐ ποιότης, τὸ δὲ ἐν τῇ ἐπιφανείᾳ ποιόν. ἢ διαιρετέον τὸ ποιόν, ὡς τὸ μὲν οὐσιῶδες ἰδιότης τις οὖσα τῆς οὐσίας, τὸ δὲ μόνον ποιόν, καθ̓ ὃ ποιὰ οὐσία, τοῦ ποιοῦ οὐ διαλλαγὴν εἰς τὴν οὐσίαν ποιοῦντος οὐδ’ ἐκ τῆς οὐσίας, ἀλλ’ οὔσης ἤδη καὶ πεπληρωμένης διάθεσίν τινα ἔξωθεν ποιοῦντος καὶ μετὰ τὴν οὐσίαν τοῦ πράγματος προσθήκην, εἴτε περὶ ψυχὴν εἴτε περὶ σῶμα γίνοιτο.

flags.taylor: elaborates the Reality into the particular thing
flags.why: The Greek says the quality is "an addition after the substance of the thing" (μετὰ τὴν οὐσίαν τοῦ πράγματος προσθήκην); it says nothing of making the particular thing.

notes: Two-footed and four-footed, the differences that divide the kind "animal", are the stock examples of Aristotle (Metaphysics VII.12).

paragraphs.modern: But what if the visible white on white lead completes it? On the swan it does not, since a swan could come to be not white; but on white lead it does. And heat does on fire. But what if someone said that fieriness is the substance, and something answering to it on the white lead? Still, the fieriness or heat of the visible fire completes it, and the whiteness the other. The same things, then, will complete and not be qualities, and will not complete and be qualities; and it is absurd to say that they are one thing where they complete and another where they do not, the nature being the same.
paragraphs.greek: ἀλλ’ εἰ καὶ τὸ ὁρώμενον λευκὸν ἐπὶ τοῦ ψιμμυθίου συμπληρωτικὸν εἴη αὐτοῦ; ἐπὶ μὲν γὰρ τοῦ κύκνου οὐ συμπληρωτικόν: γένοιτο γὰρ ἂν καὶ οὐ λευκός: ἀλλ’ ἐπὶ τοῦ ψιμμυθίου. καὶ τοῦ πυρὸς δὲ ἡ θερμότης. ἀλλ’ εἴ τις λέγοι τὴν πυρότητα τὴν οὐσίαν εἶναι καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ ψιμμυθίου τὸ ἀνάλογον; ἀλλ’ ὅμως τοῦ ὁρωμένου πυρὸς πυρότης ἢ θερμότης συμπληροῦσα καὶ ἡ λευκότης ἐπὶ τοῦ ἑτέρου. αἱ αὐταὶ τοίνυν συμπληρώσουσι καὶ οὐ ποιότητες, καὶ οὐ συμπληρώσουσι καὶ ποιότητες: καὶ ἄτοπον ἐν μὲν οἷς συμπληροῦσι λέγειν ἄλλο εἶναι, ἐν δὲ οἷς μὴ ἄλλο, τῆς αὐτῆς φύσεως οὔσης.
notes: White lead (ψιμμύθιον) is lead carbonate, ground for a white paint and for women's face powder; its whiteness is what it is.

paragraphs.modern: Or are the forming principles that made them wholly of substance, while the things they bring about are there a "something", but here qualified, not a "something"? Hence we always go wrong about the "something": in seeking it we slip away and are carried down into the qualified. For fire is not what we call it when we look to the quality: fire is a substance; but what we see now, and look to when we speak, leads us away from the "something" and defines the qualified. And with things perceived by the senses this is reasonable: none of them is a substance, but affections of it. Hence that question too: how does substance come from what are not substances? It was said that what comes to be need not be the same as what it comes from; but now we must say that what comes to be is not a substance either. But how do we say that what we called substance there comes from what is not substance? We shall say that substance there, which has being more properly and more unmixed, is substance as being among the differences of being; or rather, it is called substance with the addition of activities: it seems to be the completion of being, but is perhaps more lacking by the addition and by not being simple, standing already away from being.
paragraphs.greek: ἀλλ’ ἄρα τοὺς μὲν λόγους τοὺς ποιήσαντας αὐτὰ οὐσιώδεις ὅλους, τὰ δὲ ἀποτελέσματα ἔχειν ἤδη τὰ ἐκεῖ τὶ τὰ δ’ ἐνταῦθα ποιά, οὐ τί. ὅθεν καὶ ἁμαρτάνειν ἡμᾶς ἀεὶ περὶ τὸ τὶ ἀπολισθαίνοντας ἐν ταῖς ζητήσεσιν αὐτοῦ καὶ εἰς τὸ ποιὸν καταφερομένους. οὐ γὰρ εἶναι τὸ πῦρ ὃ λέγομεν εἰς τὸ ποιὸν ἀφορῶντες, ἀλλὰ τὸ μὲν εἶναι οὐσίαν, ἃ δὲ νῦν βλέπομεν, εἰς ἃ καὶ ἀφορῶντες λέγομεν, ἀπάγειν ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ τοῦ τὶ καὶ ὁρίζεσθαι τὸ ποιόν: καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν αἰσθητῶν εὐλόγως, οὐδὲν γὰρ αὐτῶν οὐσίαν εἶναι, ἀλλ’ αὐτῆς πάθη. ὅθεν κἀκεῖνο, πῶς ἐξ οὐκ οὐσιῶν οὐσία. ἐλέγετο μὲν οὖν, ὅτι οὐ δεῖ τὸ αὐτὸ τὸ γινόμενον εἶναι τοῖς ἐξ ὧν: νῦν δὲ λέγειν δεῖ, ὅτι οὐδὲ τὸ γενόμενον οὐσία. ἀλλὰ πῶς ἐκεῖ ἣν ἐλέγομεν οὐσίαν ἐξ οὐκ οὐσίας λέγομεν; τὴν γὰρ οὐσίαν φήσομεν ἐκεῖ κυριώτερον καὶ ἀμιγέστερον ἔχουσαν τὸ ὂν εἶναι οὐσίαν ὡς ἐν διαφοραῖς τοῦ ὄντος, μᾶλλον δὲ μετὰ προσθήκης ἐνεργειῶν λεγομένην οὐσίαν, τελείωσιν μὲν δοκοῦσαν εἶναι ἐκείνου, τάχα δ’ ἐνδεεστέραν τῇ προσθήκῃ καὶ τῷ οὐχ ἁπλῷ, ἀλλ’ ἤδη ἀφισταμένην τούτου.

flags.taylor: (not a combination of material phenomena)
flags.why: The words in brackets are MacKenna's; the Greek says only "fire is a substance".

flags.taylor: from the pure Being which is above Reality
flags.why: MacKenna's gloss in brackets; the Greek asks only how substance there comes "from what is not substance" (ἐξ οὐκ οὐσίας), being and its activities.

flags.taylor: though in the truth it is a diminution
flags.why: The Greek hedges: substance is "perhaps" (τάχα) more lacking than being; MacKenna makes it certain.

notes: The "something" (τὸ τί) and the "qualified" (τὸ ποιόν) are Aristotle's categories of substance and quality (Categories 4, 1b25-27); the Stoics too named the substrate and the qualified as two of their kinds.

paragraphs.modern: But we must look into what quality is on the whole: for once we know what it is, the difficulties may rather stop. First, then, we must ask whether the same thing is to be set down sometimes as only a quality and sometimes as completing a substance, without being troubled that a quality completes not a substance but rather a qualified substance. In the qualified substance, then, the substance, and what it is, must come before its being qualified. In fire, then, what is the substance, before the qualified substance? Is it the body? Then body will be the substance, and fire a hot body, and the whole not a substance; and the hot will be in it as the snub nose is in you. Take away, then, heat, brightness and lightness, which do seem to be qualities, and resistance, and what is left is what is extended three ways, and matter is the substance. But that does not seem right: the form is rather the substance. But the form is a quality. No: the form is not a quality but a forming principle.
paragraphs.greek: ἀλλὰ περὶ τῆς ποιότητος σκεπτέον τί ὅλως: τάχα γὰρ γνωσθὲν ὅ τι ἐστὶ μᾶλλον παύσει τὰς ἀπορίας. πρῶτον οὗν ἐκεῖνο ζητητέον, εἰ τὸ αὐτὸ θετέον ὁτὲ μὲν ποιὸν μόνον, ὁτὲ δὲ συμπληροῦν οὐσίαν, οὐ δυσχεράναντας ποιὸν οὐ συμπληρωτικὸν οὐσίας εἶναι, ἀλλὰ ποιᾶς μᾶλλον οὐσίας. δεῖ τοίνυν ἐπὶ τῆς ποιᾶς οὐσίας τὴν οὐσίαν πρὸ τοῦ ποιὰν εἶναι καὶ τὸ τί ἐστι. τί οὖν ἐπὶ τοῦ πυρὸς πρὸ τῆς ποιᾶς οὐσίας ἡ οὐσία; ἆρα τὸ σῶμα; τὸ σῶμα τοίνυν οὐσία ἔσται, τὸ δὲ πῦρ σῶμα θερμὸν καὶ οὐκ οὐσία τὸ ὅλον, ἀλλ’ οὕτω τὸ θερμὸν ἐν αὐτῷ, ὡς καὶ ἐν σοὶ τὸ σιμόν. ἀφαιρεθείσης τοίνυν θερμότητος καὶ τοῦ λαμπροῦ καὶ κούφου, ἃ δὴ δοκεῖ ποιὰ εἶναι, καὶ ἀντιτυπίας τὸ τριχῆ διαστατὸν καταλείπεται καὶ ἡ ὕλη οὐσία. ἀλλ’ οὐ δοκεῖ: τὸ γὰρ εἶδος μᾶλλον οὐσία. ἀλλὰ τὸ εἶδος ποιότης. ἢ οὐ ποιότης, ἀλλὰ λόγος τὸ εἶδος.

flags.taylor: body being the Reality, fire is a warmed body
flags.why: The Greek says "a hot body" (σῶμα θερμόν): heat that is in it, as the snub nose is in you, not heat given to it.

notes: The snub nose, a quality that belongs only to a nose, is Aristotle's example (Metaphysics VII.5, 1030b16-1031a1); Socrates was snub-nosed (Plato, Theaetetus 143e). Body as what is extended three ways, with matter under it, is Aristotle's too (Metaphysics VII.3, 1029a11-26).

paragraphs.modern: What, then, is what comes from the forming principle and the substrate? Not what is seen and burns: that is a qualified thing. Unless someone says that burning is an activity from the forming principle; and then heating and whitening and the rest are makings, so that we shall have nowhere to leave quality. Or rather, those that are said to complete substances are not to be called qualities, since they are their activities, coming from the forming principles and from the powers of the substance; qualities are what are outside all substance, not appearing as qualities in some places and not qualities in others, but holding what is over and above, after the substance: such as virtues and vices, uglinesses and beauties, healths, and being shaped in a certain way. Triangle and square by themselves are not a quality; but being made triangular, in so far as it has been shaped, is to be called a quality: not the triangularity, but the shaping. So too the arts and the aptitudes. So quality is a disposition upon substances that already are, whether brought in or there from the beginning, such that if it were not there the substance would have nothing less. And it can be easily moved or hard to move: so it has two forms, one easily moved and one lasting.
paragraphs.greek: τὰ οὖν ἐκ τοῦ λόγου καὶ τοῦ ὑποκειμένου τί ἐστιν; οὐ γὰρ τὸ ὁρώμενον καὶ τὸ καῖον: τοῦτο δὲ ποιόν. εἰ μή τις λέγοι τὸ καίειν ἐνέργειαν ἐκ τοῦ λόγου: καὶ τὸ θερμαίνειν καὶ τὸ λευκαίνειν τοίνυν καὶ τὰ ἄλλα ποιήσεις: ὥστε τὴν ποιότητα οὐχ ἕξομεν ὅπου καταλείψομεν. ἢ ταύτας μὲν οὐ λεκτέον ποιότητας, ὅσαι λέγονται συμπληροῦν οὐσίας, εἴπερ ἐνέργειαι αὐτῶν ἀπὸ τῶν λόγων καὶ τῶν δυνάμεων τῶν οὐσιωδῶν ἰοῦσαι, ἃ δέ ἐστιν ἔξωθεν πάσης οὐσίας οὐ πῂ μὲν ποιότητες, ἄλλοις δὲ οὐ ποιότητες φανταζόμεναι, τὸ δὲ περιττὸν μετὰ τὴν οὐσίαν ἔχουσαι, οἷον καὶ ἀρεταὶ καὶ κακίαι καὶ αἴσχη καὶ κάλλη καὶ ὑγίειαι καὶ οὕτως ἐσχηματίσθαι. καὶ τρίγωνον μὲν καὶ τετράγωνον καθ̓ αὑτὸ οὐ ποιόν, τὸ δὲ τετριγωνίσθαι ᾗ μεμόρφωται ποιὸν λεκτέον, καὶ οὐ τὴν τριγωνότητα, ἀλλὰ τὴν μόρφωσιν: καὶ τὰς τέχνας δὲ καὶ τὰς ἐπιτηδειότητας: ὥστε εἶναι τὴν ποιότητα διάθεσίν τινα ἐπὶ ταῖς οὐσίαις ἤδη οὔσαις εἴτε ἐπακτὴν εἴτε ἐξ ἀρχῆς συνοῦσαν, ἣ εἰ μὴ συνῆν, οὐδὲν ἔλαττον εἶχεν ἂν ἡ οὐσία. ταύτην δὲ καὶ εὐκίνητον καὶ δυσκίνητον εἶναι: ὡς διττὸν εἶναι εἶδος, τὸ μὲν εὐκίνητον, τὸ δὲ ἔμμονον αὐτῆς.

flags.taylor: that is the something in which these qualities inhere
flags.why: The Greek says "this is a qualified thing" (τοῦτο δὲ ποιόν): what is seen and burns is already qualified, not the subject in which the qualities are.

flags.taylor: the warming and lighting and other effects of fire
flags.why: The Greek is τὸ λευκαίνειν, "whitening", not lighting.

flags.taylor: by which human beings take the quality
flags.why: The words in brackets are MacKenna's; the Greek names only "the arts and the aptitudes".

notes: Quality as a disposition easily moved, or a lasting state, is Aristotle's first kind of quality (Categories 8, 8b26-9a13), with shape his fourth (10a11-16).

paragraphs.modern: The white on you, then, is to be set down not as a quality but plainly as an activity, from a power of whitening; and there all the so-called qualities are activities, which take on being qualities from our opinion, because each is a mark of its own, as it were marking the substances off from one another and having a character proper to themselves. How, then, will quality there differ, since these too are activities? Because they do not show what kind a thing is, nor a change in the substrates, nor a character, but only what is called quality there, being activity. So when it has the distinctiveness of a substance, it is plain at once that it is not a quality; but when reason separates what is distinctive in them, not taking it away from there but rather taking it and begetting something else, it begets a quality, taking as a part of substance what appeared to it on the surface. If so, nothing prevents heat too, being inborn in fire, from being a form of fire and an activity, and not its quality; and again, taken otherwise, in something else, from being only a quality, no longer the shape of a substance but a trace only, a shadow and an image, which has left behind its own substance, whose activity it is.
paragraphs.greek: τὸ οὖν λευκὸν τὸ ἐπὶ σοὶ θετέον οὐ ποιότητα, ἀλλ’ ἐνέργειαν δηλονότι ἐκ δυνάμεως τῆς τοῦ λευκαίνειν, κἀκεῖ πάσας τὰς λεγομένας ποιότητας ἐνεργείας τὸ ποιὸν λαβούσας παρὰ τῆς ἡμετέρας δόξης τῷ ἰδιώτητα εἶναι ἑκάστην οἷον διοριζούσας τὰς οὐσίας πρὸς ἀλλήλας καὶ πρὸς ἑαυτὰς ἴδιον χαρακτῆρα ἐχούσας. τί οὖν διοίσει ποιότης ἡ ἐκεῖ; ἐνέργειαι γὰρ καὶ αὗται. ἢ ὅτι μὴ οἷόν τί ἐστι δηλοῦσιν οὐδὲ ἐναλλαγὴν τῶν ὑποκειμένων οὐδὲ χαρακτῆρα, ἀλλ’ ὅσον μόνον τὴν λεγομένην ποιότητα ἐκεῖ ἐνέργειαν οὖσαν: ὥστε τὸ μέν, ὅταν ἰδιότητα οὐσίας ἔχῃ, δῆλον αὐτόθεν ὡς οὐ ποιόν, ὅταν δὲ χωρίσῃ ὁ λόγος τὸ ἐπ’ αὐτοῖς ἴδιον οὐκ ἐκεῖθεν ἀφελών, ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον λαβὼν καὶ γεννήσας ἄλλο, ἐγέννησε ποιὸν οἷον μέρος οὐσίας λαβὼν τὸ ἐπιπολῆς φανὲν αὐτῷ. εἰ δὲ τοῦτο, οὐδὲν κωλύει καὶ τὴν θερμότητα τῷ σύμφυτον εἶναι τῷ πυρὶ εἶδός τι εἶναι τοῦ πυρὸς καὶ ἐνέργειαν καὶ οὐ ποιότητα αὐτοῦ, καὶ αὖ ἄλλως ποιότητα μόνην ἐν ἄλλῳ ληφθεῖσαν οὐκέτι μορφὴν οὐσίας οὖσαν, ἀλλὰ ἴχνος μόνον καὶ σκιὰν καὶ εἰκόνα ἀπολιποῦσαν αὑτῆς τὴν οὐσίαν, ἧς ἡ ἐνέργεια, ποιότητα εἶναι.

flags.taylor: (as do the corresponding Activities here)
flags.why: The words in brackets are MacKenna's; the Greek sets no activities here beside them.

notes: "Shadow" and "image" (σκιά, εἰκών) are the words of Plato's line in the Republic (VI, 509e-510a) for what lies below the things themselves; for Plotinus the qualities of bodies stand so to the activities of the intelligible.

paragraphs.modern: Whatever is accidental, then, and not the activities and forms of substances, while providing some shapes, is qualified: so the states and the other dispositions of the substrates are to be called qualities, but their archetypes, in which they first are, are the activities of those things. And the same thing does not become quality and not quality: what is stripped of substance is quality, what is with it is form or activity; for nothing is the same when it stays in itself and when it has fallen into another, out of being form and activity. But what is never the form of anything else, but always an accident, is purely quality, and only that.
paragraphs.greek: ὅσα οὖν συμβέβηκε καὶ μὴ ἐνέργειαι καὶ εἴδη οὐσιῶν μορφάς τινας παρεχόμενα, ποιὰ ταῦτα: οἷον καὶ αἱ ἕξεις καὶ διαθέσεις ἄλλαι τῶν ὑποκειμένων λεκτέαι ποιότητες, τὰ δὲ ἀρχέτυπα αὐτῶν, ἐν οἷς πρώτως ἐστίν, ἐνεργείας ἐκείνων. καὶ οὐ γίνεται ταὐτὸ ποιότης καὶ οὐ ποιότης, ἀλλὰ τὸ ἀπηρημωμένον οὐσίας ποιόν, τὸ δὲ σὺν ταύτῃ ἢ εἶδος ἢ ἐνέργεια: οὐδὲν γάρ ἐστι ταὐτὸν ἐν αὑτῷ μένον καὶ ἐν ἄλλῳ ἐκπεσὸν τοῦ εἶδος καὶ ἐνέργεια εἶναι. ὃ μέντοι μηδέποτε εἶδος ἄλλου, ἀλλὰ συμβεβηκὸς ἀεί, καθαρῶς ποιότης καὶ μόνον τοῦτο.

flags.taylor: other than those constituting the substratum of a thing
flags.why: The Greek says the states and dispositions "of the substrates" (τῶν ὑποκειμένων) are qualities: they are in the substrates, not set against what makes them.

paragraphs.modern: We must look into what is called the complete blending of bodies, through and through. Can a liquid mixed with a liquid go whole through whole, each through the other, or one through the other? It makes no difference which, if it happens. Those who allow only setting side by side may be let go, as mixing rather than blending, if blending must make the whole of like parts, each smallest part made of the things said to be blended. Those who blend only the qualities, and set the matter of each body side by side, bringing on to it the qualities from each, might be persuasive in attacking complete blending: because the sizes of the masses would come to be cut into pieces, if there is no gap left in either body and the division is continuous, the one sinking into the other everywhere; and further, because the blended things take up a greater place than either one, as much as the places of both together. Yet if whole had gone through whole, they say, the place of the one into which the other was thrown should stay the same. And where the place does not become greater, they blame some going out of air, in place of which the other sank in. And how could the small, stretched out in the greater, pass through the whole of it? And they say many other things.
paragraphs.greek: Περὶ τῆς δἰ ὅλων λεγομένης τῶν σωμάτων κράσεως ἐπισκεπτέον. ἆρα ἐνδέχεται ὅλον δἰ ὅλου ὑγρὸν ὑγρῷ συμμιχθὲν ἑκάτερον δἰ ἑκατέρου ἢ θάτερον διὰ θατέρου χωρεῖν; διαφέρει γὰρ οὐδὲν ὁποτερωσοῦν, εἰ γίγνοιτο. οἱ μὲν γὰρ τῇ παραθέσει διδόντες ὡς μιγνύντες μᾶλλον ἢ κιρνάντες ἐατέοι, εἴπερ δεῖ τὴν κρᾶσιν ὁμοιομερὲς τὸ πᾶν ποιεῖν, καὶ ἕκαστον μέρος τὸ σμικρότατον ἐκ τῶν κεκρᾶσθαι λεγομένων εἶναι. οἱ μὲν οὖν τὰς ποιότητας μόνας κιρνάντες τὴν δὲ ὕλην παρατιθέντες ἑκατέρου τοῦ σώματος καὶ ἐπ’ αὐτῶν ἐπάγοντες τὰς παῤ ἑκατέρου ποιότητας πιθανοὶ ἂν εἶεν τῷ διαβάλλειν τὴν δἰ ὅλων κρᾶσιν τῷ τε εἰς τομὰς τὰ μεγέθη συμβαίνειν τῶν ὄγκων ἰέναι, εἰ μηδὲν διάλειμμα μηδετέρῳ τῶν σωμάτων γίγνοιτο, εἰ συνεχὴς ἔσται ἡ διαίρεσις τῷ κατὰ πᾶν τὴν διάδυσιν γίνεσθαι θατέρῳ εἰς θάτερον, καὶ δή, ὅταν τὰ κραθέντα μείζω τόπον κατέχῃ ἢ θάτερον καὶ τοσοῦτον, ὅσον συνελθόντα τὸν ἑκατέρου τόπον. καίτοι, εἰ δἰ ὅλου ὅλον ἦν διεληλυθός, τὸν τοῦ ἑτέρου ἔδει, φασί, μένειν τὸν αὐτόν, εἰς ὃ θάτερον ἐνεβλήθη. οὗ δὲ μὴ μείζων ὁ τόπος γίνεται, ἀέρος τινὰς ἐξόδους αἰτιῶνται, ἀνθ̓ ὧν ἐσέδυ θάτερον. καὶ τὸ σμικρὸν δὲ ἐν τῷ μείζονι πῶς ἂν ἐκταθὲν δἰ ὅλου χωρήσειε; καὶ πολλὰ ἄλλα λέγουσιν.

flags.taylor: must be whittled away if there is to be mixture without any gap
flags.why: The Greek says the masses would be cut "into pieces" (εἰς τομάς), divided without end, not whittled.

notes: "Complete blending" (κρᾶσις δι’ ὅλων) is the Stoics': two bodies, wine and water, wholly through each other, so that a drop of wine could blend with the whole sea (Diogenes Laertius VII.151; Plutarch, On common conceptions 37, 1078e). Setting side by side (παράθεσις), as of grains, the Stoics called mixing, not blending. Blending only the qualities is the Peripatetic answer: Aristotle says a drop of wine in ten thousand measures of water does not blend but turns into water (On Generation and Corruption I.10, 328a23-28), and Alexander of Aphrodisias argued against the Stoics in his On mixture.

paragraphs.modern: Those who bring in complete blending, on the other hand, could say that the bodies are cut but not used up in the cuts, even when the blending is through and through; for they will say that sweat too does not make cuts in the body, nor is the body pierced with holes. And if someone says that nothing prevents nature having made it so, so that sweat may pass through, still with things made by craft, when they are thin and continuous, a liquid is seen to wet them through and flow through to the other side. "But since they are bodies, how can this happen? For it is not easy to conceive of passing through without cutting; and cutting everywhere, they will plainly destroy one another." When they say that increases often do not happen, they give the others the going out of air to blame. As to the increase in place, it is hard; but still, what prevents saying that, since each body brings its size along with its other qualities, the increase comes of necessity? For size is not destroyed either, any more than the other qualities; and as there a different form of quality comes, mixed from both, so a different size, the size from both that the mixture makes.
paragraphs.greek: οἱ δ’ αὖ τὴν δἰ ὅλων κρᾶσιν εἰσάγοντες τέμνεσθαι μὲν καὶ μὴ εἰς τομὰς ἀναλίσκεσθαι λέγειν ἂν δύναιντο καὶ δἰ ὅλων τῆς κράσεως γιγνομένης: ἐπεὶ καὶ τοὺς ἱδρῶτας οὐ τοῦ σώματος τομὰς ποιεῖν οὐδ’ αὖ κατατετρῆσθαι φήσουσι. καὶ γὰρ εἴ τις λέγοι μηδὲν κωλύειν τὴν φύσιν οὕτω πεποιηκέναι τοῦ διιέναι τοὺς ἱδρῶτας χάριν, ἀλλὰ ἐπὶ τῶν τεχνητῶν, ὅταν λεπτὰ ᾖ καὶ συνεχῆ, ὁρᾶσθαι τὸ ὑγρὸν δἰ ὅλου δεῦον αὐτὰ καὶ διάρρεον ἐπὶ θάτερα: ἀλλὰ σωμάτων ὄντων πῶς οἷόν τε τοῦτο γίγνεσθαι; ὡς διιέναι μὴ τέμνοντα ἐπινοῆσαι οὐ ῥᾴδιον: τέμνοντα δὲ κατὰ πᾶν ἀναιρήσει ἄλληλα δηλονότι. τὰς δὲ αὔξας ὅταν λέγωσι μὴ γίγνεσθαι πολλαχοῦ, διδόασι τοῖς ἑτέροις ἀέρων ἐξόδους αἰτιᾶσθαι. πρός τε τὴν τῶν τόπων αὔξησιν χαλεπῶς μέν, ὅμως δὲ τί κωλύει λέγειν συνεισφερομένου ἑκατέρου σώματος καὶ τὸ μέγεθος μετὰ τῶν ἄλλων ποιοτήτων ἐξ ἀνάγκης τὴν αὔξην γίνεσθαι; μὴ γὰρ μηδὲ τοῦτο ἀπόλλυσθαι, ὥσπερ οὐδὲ τὰς ἄλλας ποιότητας, καὶ ὥσπερ ἐκεῖ ποιότητος ἄλλο εἶδος μικτὸν ἐξ ἀμφοῖν, οὕτω καὶ μέγεθος ἄλλο: οὗ δὴ τὸ μῖγμα ποιεῖ τὸ ἐξ ἀμφοῖν μέγεθος.
notes: Sweat passing through the skin, which has no holes we can see, was used on both sides; the Stoics took it as a body through a body.

paragraphs.modern: But here the others might say to them: "If matter lies beside matter, and mass beside mass, with which the size goes, you would be saying what we say; but if matter too goes through and through, with the size that is first upon it, it would not happen as when line lies next to line, joining at the ends by their points, where there would be an increase, but as when line is laid on line, so that there is no increase." But the less goes through the whole of the greater, and the smallest through the greatest, where it is plain that it is blended. With things not seen it is possible to say that it does not reach everywhere; but where it plainly happens, it could not be said. And when they speak of the stretching of masses, they would not say very persuasive things, stretching the smallest mass so far: for they do not give the body a greater size by changing it, as if air came to be from water.
paragraphs.greek: ἀλλ’ ἐνταῦθ̓ ἂν πρὸς αὐτοὺς οἱ ἕτεροι λέγοιεν, ὡς, εἰ μὲν ἡ ὕλη τῇ ὕλῃ παράκειται καὶ ὁ ὄγκος τῷ ὄγκῳ, ᾧ. σύνεστι τὸ μέγεθος, τὸ ἡμέτερον ἂν λέγοιτε: εἰ δὲ δἰ ὅλου καὶ ἡ ὕλη μετὰ τοῦ ἐπ’ αὐτῇ πρώτως μεγέθους, οὐχ οὕτως ἂν γένοιτο ὡς γραμμὴ γραμμῇ ἐφεξῆς ἂν κέοιτο κατὰ τὰ πέρατα τοῖς σημείοις ἑαυτῶν συνάψασαι, οὗ δὴ αὔξη ἂν γίνοιτο, ἀλλ’ ἐκείνως ὡς ἂν γραμμὴ γραμμῇ ἐφαρμοσθείη, ὥστε αὔξην μὴ γίνεσθαι. τὸ δὲ ἔλαττον διὰ παντὸς τοῦ μείζονος καὶ τοῦ μεγίστου τὸ μικρότατον χωρεῖ, ἐφ̓ ὧν φανερὸν ὅτι κίρναται. ἐπὶ γὰρ τῶν ἀδήλων ἔξεστι λέγειν μὴ εἰς πᾶν φθάνειν, ἀλλ’ ἐφ̓ ὧν γε φανερῶς συμβαίνει, οὐ λέγοιτ̓ ἄν. καὶ λέγοντες ἐκτάσεις τῶν ὄγκων, οὐ σφόδρα πιθανὰ λέγοιεν ἂν εἰς τοσοῦτον τὸν σμικρότατον ὄγκον ἐκτείνοντες: οὐδὲ γὰρ μεταβάλλοντες τὸ σῶμα μέγεθος αὐτῷ πλέον διδόασιν, ὥσπερ εἰ ἐξ ὕδατος ἀὴρ γίγνοιτο.

flags.taylor: one substance sinking its original magnitude in the other
flags.why: The Greek says "if matter too goes through and through, with the size that is first upon it" (μετὰ τοῦ ἐπ’ αὐτῇ πρώτως μεγέθους): the matter goes with its size, rather than sinking it.

paragraphs.modern: This itself must be looked into on its own, what happens when the mass of water that was becomes air, and how the greater is in what has come to be; for now let these things be said, among many others said by each side. Let us look for ourselves at what we should say about this: what opinion agrees with what is said, or what other will appear beside those now said. When water runs through wool, then, or papyrus lets the water in it drip out, how does the whole watery body not pass through it? Or even when it does not run, how shall we join matter to matter and mass to mass, and make only the qualities blend? For the water's matter will not lie outside the papyrus, nor in some gaps in it: for all of it is wet, and nowhere is matter empty of the watery quality. And if the matter is everywhere with the quality, the water is everywhere in the papyrus.
paragraphs.greek: τοῦτο δὲ αὐτὸ ἐφ̓ ἑαυτοῦ ζητητέον, τί συμβαίνει, ὅταν ὅσπερ ἦν ὄγκος ὕδατος ἀὴρ γίγνηται, πῶς τὸ μεῖζον ἐν τῷ γενομένῳ: νῦν δὲ τὰ μὲν εἰρήσθω πολλῶν καὶ ἄλλων παῤ ἑκατέρων λεγομένων. ἡμεῖς δὲ ἐφ̓ ἑαυτῶν σκοπῶμεν, τί χρὴ λέγειν περὶ τούτου, τίς δόξα σύμφωνος τοῖς λεγομένοις ἢ καὶ τίς ἄλλη παρὰ τὰς νῦν λεγομένας φανεῖται; ὅταν τοίνυν διὰ τοῦ ἐρίου ῥέῃ τὸ ὕδωρ ἢ ἡ βίβλος ἐκστάζῃ τὸ ἐν αὐτῇ ὕδωρ, πῶς οὐ τὸ πᾶν ὑδάτινον σῶμα δίεισι δἰ αὐτῆς; ἢ καὶ ὅταν μὴ ῥέῃ, πῶς συνάψομεν τὴν ὕλην τῇ ὕλῃ καὶ τὸν ὄγκον τῷ ὄγκῳ, τὰς δὲ ποιότητας μόνας ἐν συγκράσει ποιησόμεθα; οὐ γὰρ δὴ ἔξω τῆς βίβλου ἡ τοῦ ὕδατος ὕλη παρακείσεται οὐδ’ αὖ ἔν τισι διαστήμασιν αὐτῆς: πᾶσα γὰρ ὑγρά ἐστι καὶ οὐδαμοῦ ὕλη κενὴ ὑδατίνης ποιότητος. εἰ δὲ πανταχοῦ ἡ ὕλη μετὰ τῆς ποιότητος, πανταχοῦ τῆς βίβλου τὸ ὕδωρ.

flags.taylor: without regard to the agreement or disagreement of that theory
flags.why: The Greek asks "what opinion agrees with what is said, or what other will appear" (τίς δόξα σύμφωνος τοῖς λεγομένοις): the agreement is what Plotinus looks for.

flags.taylor: when papyrus-pulp gives up its moisture
flags.why: The Greek is ἡ βίβλος, papyrus, the reed or a sheet of it; the "pulp" is MacKenna's.

paragraphs.modern: "Not the water, but the water's quality." But where is the water, then? And how is the mass not the same? Or what was added stretched the papyrus: for it took size from what came in. But if it took it, some mass was added; and if added, it was not swallowed up in the other; so the matter must be in one place and in another. Or what prevents that, as one body gives some of its quality to the other and takes from it, so too with size? For a quality coming together with a quality is not that quality but with another, and in being with another, not being pure, is not wholly that, but has been dimmed; but a size coming together with another size does not vanish.
paragraphs.greek: ἢ οὐ τὸ ὕδωρ, ἀλλ’ ἡ τοῦ ὕδατος ποιότης. ἀλλὰ ποῦ ὄντος τοῦ ὕδατος; πῶς οὖν οὐχ ὁ αὐτὸς ὄγκος; ἢ ἐξέτεινε τὴν βίβλον τὸ προστεθέν: ἔλαβε γὰρ μέγεθος παρὰ τοῦ εἰσελθόντος. ἀλλ’ εἰ ἔλαβε, προσετέθη τις ὄγκος: εἰ δὲ προσετέθη, οὐ κατεπόθη ἐν τῷ ἑτέρῳ, δεῖ οὖν ἐν ἄλλῳ καὶ ἄλλῳ τὴν ὕλην εἶναι. ἢ τί κωλύει, ὥσπερ δίδωσι τῆς ποιότητος καὶ λαμβάνει σῶμα θάτερον παρὰ θατέρου, οὕτω καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ μεγέθους; ποιότης μὲν γὰρ ποιότητι συνελθοῦσα οὐκ ἐκείνη οὖσα, ἀλλὰ μετ’ ἄλλης, ἐν τῷ μετ’ ἄλλης εἶναι οὐ καθαρὰ οὖσα οὐκ ἔστι παντελῶς ἐκείνη, ἀλλ’ ἠμαύρωται: μέγεθος δὲ συνελθὸν ἄλλῳ μεγέθει οὐκ ἀφανίζεται.

flags.taylor: communicate quality and receive matter
flags.why: The Greek says "one body gives of the quality and takes from the other" (δίδωσι τῆς ποιότητος καὶ λαμβάνει σῶμα θάτερον παρὰ θατέρου): "body" is what gives and takes, not matter received.

paragraphs.modern: How it is said that body passing through body must make cuts, one might stop and ask: for we too say that the qualities pass through bodies and make no cuts. Because they are bodiless? But if matter itself is bodiless too, why, matter being bodiless and the qualities too, if they were such as to be few, do they not pass through with the matter in the same way? Do solids not pass through because they have qualities such that they are stopped from passing through, or because many together cannot do this with matter? If, then, the number of qualities makes what is called a dense body, the number would be the cause; but if density is a quality of its own, like what they call corporeity, the cause is that quality. So qualities will not make the mixing as qualities, but as qualities of a certain kind; nor again will matter fail to mix as matter, but as matter with a certain quality; and most of all if it has no size of its own, except that it does not throw off size. Let these things, then, be gone through in this way too, as difficulties.
paragraphs.greek: τὸ δὲ σῶμα χωροῦν διὰ σώματος πάντως τομὰς ποιεῖν πῶς λέγεται, ἐπιστήσειεν ἄν τις: ἐπεὶ καὶ αὐτοὶ τὰς ποιότητας διὰ τῶν σωμάτων χωρεῖν λέγομεν καὶ οὐ τομὰς ποιεῖν. ἢ ὅτι ἀσώματοι. ἀλλ’ εἰ ἡ ὕλη καὶ αὐτὴ ἀσώματος, διὰ τί τῆς ὕλης ἀσωμάτου οὔσης καὶ τῶν ποιοτήτων, εἰ τοιαῦται εἶεν ὡς ὀλίγαι εἶναι, οὐ μετὰ τῆς ὕλης τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον διίασι; μὴ διιέναι δὲ τὰ στερεά, ὅτι τοιαύτας ἔχει τὰς ποιότητας ὡς κωλυθῆναι διιέναι, ἢ πολλὰς ὁμοῦ ἀδυνατεῖν μετὰ τῆς ὕλης ποιεῖν τοῦτο; εἰ μὲν οὖν τὸ πλῆθος τῶν ποιοτήτων τὸ πυκνὸν λεγόμενον σῶμα ποιεῖ, τὸ πλῆθος ἂν εἴη αἴτιον: εἰ δὲ πυκνότης ἰδία ποιότης ἐστίν, ὥσπερ καὶ ἣν λέγουσι σωματότητα, ἡ ἰδία ποιότης: ὥστε οὐχ ᾗ ποιότητες τὴν μῖξιν ποιήσονται, ἀλλ’ ᾗ τοιαίδε, οὐδ’ αὖ ἡ ὕλη ᾗ ὕλη οὐ μιχθήσεται, ἀλλ’ ᾗ μετὰ τοιᾶσδε ποιότητος, καὶ μάλιστα, εἰ μέγεθος οἰκεῖον οὐκ ἔχει ἀλλ’ ἢ μὴ ἀποβαλοῦσα τὸ μέγεθος. ταῦτα μὲν οὖν ἔστω καὶ οὕτω διηπορημένα.

flags.taylor: how we came to say that body passing through
flags.why: The Greek says "one might stop and ask how it is said" (πῶς λέγεται): the claim that body cuts body is the opponents', not Plotinus' own.

notes: That matter is bodiless, and has no size of its own but takes it, is argued in II.4 (chapters 8-12), Taylor's On matter.

paragraphs.modern: Since we have mentioned corporeity, we must look into whether corporeity is what is made up of all the qualities together with matter, or a form and a forming principle which, coming to be in matter, makes a body. If body is what is made up of all the qualities together with matter, corporeity would be that same thing. And if it is a forming principle which, coming on, makes the body, plainly the principle holds all the qualities embraced in itself. But this principle, if it is not merely like a definition showing what the thing is, but a principle making a thing, must not take in matter along with itself, but be about matter, and, coming to be in it, complete the body; and the body is matter and the principle in it, while the principle itself, being a form, is seen bare, without matter, even if it is as inseparable as can be. For the separable principle is another, the one in intellect; and it is in intellect because it is itself intellect. But these things belong elsewhere.
paragraphs.greek: ἐπεὶ δὲ ἐμνήσθημεν σωματότητος, ἐπισκεπτέον, πότερα ἡ σωματότης ἐστὶ τὸ ἐκ πάντων σὺν ὕλῃ συγκείμενον ἢ εἶδός τι καὶ λόγος τις, ὃς ἐγγενόμενος τῇ ὕλῃ σῶμα ποιεῖ. εἰ μὲν οὖν τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ σῶμα τὸ ἐκ πασῶν τῶν ποιοτήτων σὺν ὕλῃ συγκείμενον, ταὐτὸ ἂν εἴη ἡ σωματότης. καὶ εἰ λόγος δὲ εἴη, ὃς προσελθὼν ποιεῖ τὸ σῶμα, δηλονότι ὁ λόγος ἐμπεριλαβὼν ἔχει τὰς ποιότητας ἁπάσας. δεῖ δὲ τὸν λόγον τοῦτον, εἰ μή ἐστιν ἄλλως ὥσπερ ὁρισμὸς δηλωτικὸς τοῦ τί ἔστι τὸ πρᾶγμα, ἀλλὰ λόγος ποιῶν πρᾶγμα, μὴ τὴν ὕλην συμπεριειληφέναι, ἀλλὰ περὶ ὕλην εἶναι καὶ ἐγγενόμενον ἀποτελεῖν τὸ σῶμα, καὶ εἶναι μὲν τὸ σῶμα ὕλην καὶ λόγον ἐνόντα, αὐτὸν δὲ εἶδος ὄντα ἄνευ ὕλης ψιλὸν θεωρεῖσθαι, κἂν ὅτι μάλιστα ἀχώριστος αὐτὸς ᾖ. ὁ γὰρ χωριστὸς ἄλλος, ὁ ἐν νῷ: ἐν νῷ δέ, ὅτι καὶ αὐτὸς νοῦς. ἀλλὰ ταῦτα ἄλλοθι.

flags.taylor: that other Principle in man
flags.why: The Greek speaks of "the separable" forming principle, "the one in intellect" (ὁ ἐν νῷ); nothing is said of man.

notes: A definition (ὁρισμός) that shows what a thing is, against a principle that makes it: Aristotle's formula (λόγος) is both the definition and the form (Metaphysics VII.10-11).

paragraphs.modern: Do distant things look smaller, and things far apart seem to have little between them, while things near look as large as they are, and as far apart as they are? Distant things seem smaller to those who see them because the light wants to be drawn together towards the sight and to the size of the pupil; and the further off the matter of what is seen is, the more the form arrives as if alone, stripped of the form of its size and of its quality too, so that only its forming principle arrives. Or else because we perceive how great a size is by going through it and passing over it part by part: so it must be present and near to be known for how great it is. Or else because size is seen by accident, colour being seen first. Near, then, we know how much is coloured; far off, only that it is coloured; and the parts, divided with it by quantity, do not give an exact discerning of the quantity, since the colours themselves arrive faint. What wonder, then, if sizes too, like sounds, are smaller as their form comes faint? For there too hearing seeks the form, and perceives the size by accident.
paragraphs.greek: Ἆρα τὰ πόρρω φαίνεται ἐλάττω καὶ τὰ πολὺ ἀφεστηκότα ὀλίγον δοκεῖ ἔχειν τὸ μεταξύ, τὰ δὲ ἐγγύθεν ἡλίκα ἐστὶ φαίνεται, καὶ ὅσην ἔχει τὴν ἀπόστασιν; ἐλάττω μὲν δοκεῖ τοῖς ὁρῶσι τὰ πόρρω, ὅτι συναιρεῖσθαι πρὸς τὴν ὄψιν ἐθέλει καὶ πρὸς τὸ μέγεθος τῆς κόρης τὸ φῶς — καὶ ὅσῳ ἂν πόρρω ἡ ὕλη ᾖ τοῦ ὁρωμένου, τόσῳ τὸ εἶδος οἷον μεμονωμένον ἀφικνεῖται καὶ τοῦ πηλίκου εἴδους καὶ αὖ τοῦ ποιοῦ, ὡς τὸν λόγον αὐτοῦ ἀφικνεῖσθαι μόνον: ἢ καί, ὅτι τὸ μὲν μέγεθος ἐν διεξόδῳ καὶ ἐπελεύσει καθ̓ ἕκαστον μέρος ὅσον ἐστὶν αἰσθανόμεθα — παρεῖναι οὖν δεῖ αὐτὸ καὶ πλησίον εἶναι, ἵνα γνωσθῇ ὅσον: ἢ καί, ὅτι κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς ὁρᾶται τὸ μέγεθος τοῦ χρώματος πρώτως θεωρουμένου. πλησίον μὲν οὖν ὅσον κέχρωσται γινώσκεται, πόρρω δὲ ὅτι κέχρωσται, τὰ δὲ μέρη κατὰ ποσὸν συνδιαιρούμενα οὐκ ἀκριβῆ δίδωσι τὴν τοῦ ποσοῦ διάγνωσιν: ἐπεὶ καὶ τὰ χρώματα αὐτὰ ἀμυδρὰ προσέρχεται. τί οὖν θαυμαστόν, εἰ καὶ τὰ μεγέθη, ὥσπερ καὶ αἱ φωναί, ἐλάττω, ὅσῳ ἂν τὸ εἶδος αὐτῶν ἀμυδρὸν ἴῃ; εἶδος γὰρ κἀκεῖ ἡ ἀκοὴ ζητεῖ, τὸ δὲ μέγεθος κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς αἰσθάνεται.

flags.taylor: stripped, so to speak, of magnitude as of all other quality
flags.why: The Greek goes on: "so that only its forming principle arrives" (ὡς τὸν λόγον αὐτοῦ ἀφικνεῖσθαι μόνον); MacKenna leaves it out.

flags.taylor: by observing the salience and recession of its several parts
flags.why: The Greek says we know a size "by going through it and passing over it" part by part (ἐν διεξόδῳ καὶ ἐπελεύσει): sight travels over the parts; nothing is said of parts standing out or falling back.

notes: Size is one of Aristotle's "common sensibles", perceived by more than one sense, and colour the "proper sensible" of sight (On the Soul II.6, 418a7-20; III.1, 425a14-20).

paragraphs.modern: But as for hearing, does it perceive size by accident? For to what does the size in a sound belong first, as the size of what is seen seems to belong to touch? Or rather hearing perceives the seeming size not by quantity but by more and less, not by accident, as the strength of it, just as taste perceives the strength of the sweet; but the size of a sound in the proper sense is how far it reaches; and this it would signify by accident from the strength, but not exactly. For the strength is the same at each point, while the amount goes over all the place the sound has covered. "But colours are not small but faint, while sizes are small." Or rather what is common to both is the less. In colour, the less is faint; in size, the less is small; and the size, following the colour, is lessened in proportion.
paragraphs.greek: ἀλλὰ περὶ τῆς ἀκοῆς, εἰ τὸ μέγεθος κατὰ συμβεβηκός: τίνι γὰρ πρώτως τὸ ἐν τῇ φωνῇ μέγεθος, ὥσπερ δοκεῖ τῇ ἁφῇ τὸ ὁρώμενον; ἢ τὸ δοκοῦν μέγεθος ἡ ἀκοὴ οὐ κατὰ τὸ ποσόν, ἀλλὰ κατὰ τὸ μᾶλλον καὶ ἧττον, οὐ κατὰ συμβεβηκός, οἷον τὸ σφόδρα, ὡς καὶ ἡ γεῦσις τὸ σφόδρα τοῦ γλυκέος κατὰ συμβεβηκός: τὸ δὲ κυρίως μέγεθος φωνῆς τὸ ἐφ̓ ὅσον: τοῦτο δὲ κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς ἐκ τοῦ σφόδρα σημήνειεν ἄν, οὐκ ἀκριβῶς δέ. τὸ μὲν γὰρ σφόδρα ἑκάστῳ τὸ αὐτό, τὸ δὲ εἰς πλῆθος εἰς ἅπαντα τὸν τόπον, ὃν ἐπέσχεν. ἀλλ’ οὐ σμικρὰ τὰ χρώματα, ἀλλὰ ἀμυδρά, τὰ δὲ μεγέθη σμικρά. ἢ ἐν ἀμφοτέροις κοινὸν τὸ ἧττόν ἐστι. χρῶμα μὲν οὖν τὸ ἧττον ἀμυδρόν, μέγεθος δὲ τὸ ἧττον σμικρόν, καὶ ἑπόμενον τῷ χρώματι τὸ μέγεθος ἀνὰ λόγον ἠλάττωται.

flags.taylor: exactly as the palate perceives by no indirect knowledge
flags.why: The Greek of the Workshop ends the comparison with "by accident" (κατὰ συμβεβηκός); the modern version, like MacKenna, takes the sense to be that taste, like hearing, knows the strength directly, and leaves the words out.

paragraphs.modern: The experience is clearer with things that are varied: mountains, say, with many houses, a host of trees and many other things; each of these, if seen, lets one measure the whole from the things seen one by one; but when the form does not come for each, sight, which measures by each, is deprived of knowing how great the whole underlying size is. For even things near, when they are varied and one's glance falls on them all at once and not all the forms are seen, would look smaller in proportion to how much of each is stolen from view; but when all are seen, they are measured exactly and known for how great they are. And sizes of one look and one colour deceive about their quantity too, since sight cannot measure them part by part at all, because, measuring part by part, it slips off, for it has no difference at which to stop at each part. And the distant looks near because the stretch between is drawn together, how great it is, for the same reason. For how great the near is does not escape us, for the same reasons; but not going through the distant part of the interval, what it is like in form, sight could not say how great it is in size either.
paragraphs.greek: σαφέστερον δὲ ἐπὶ τῶν ποικίλων γίνεται τὸ πάθος: οἷον ὀρῶν ἐχόντων πολλὰς οἰκήσεις καὶ δένδρων πλῆθος καὶ ἄλλα πολλά, ὧν ἕκαστον, εἰ μὲν ὁρῷτο, δίδωσιν ἐκ τῶν ὁρωμένων ἑκάστων μετρεῖν τὸ ὅλον: τοῦ δὲ εἴδους καθ̓ ἕκαστον οὐκ ἰόντος ἀπεστέρηται τοῦ καθ̓ ἕκαστον ὄψις μετροῦσα τὸ ὑποκείμενον μέγεθος τὸ πᾶν ὅσον ἐστὶ γινώσκειν. ἐπεὶ καὶ τὰ πλησίον, ὅταν ποικίλα ᾖ ἀθρόως τε γίνηται ἡ ἐπιβολὴ πρὸς αὐτὰ καὶ μὴ πάντα τὰ εἴδη ὁρῷτο, ἐλάττω ἂν φανείη κατὰ λόγον, ὅσον ἂν ἕκαστον κλαπῇ ἐν τῇ θέᾳ: ὅταν δὲ πάντα ὀφθῇ, ἀκριβῶς μετρηθέντα ὅσα ἐστὶ γινώσκεται. ὅσα δὲ τῶν μεγεθῶν ὁμοειδῆ ὁμοιόχροα ὄντα, ψεύδεται καὶ ταῦτα τὸ ποσὸς αὐτῆς οὐ κατὰ μέρος πάνυ τι μετρεῖν δυναμένης τῆς ὄψεως, ὅτι ἀπολισθάνει κατὰ μέρος μετροῦσα, ὅτι μὴ ἔχει ἵστασθαι καθ̓ ἕκαστον μέρος τῇ διαφορᾷ. ἐγγύθεν δὲ τὸ πόρρω, ὅτι τὸ μεταξὺ συναιρεῖται ὅσον ἐστὶ κατὰ τὴν αὐτὴν αἰτίαν. τὸ μὲν γὰρ πλησίον ὅσον ἐστὶν οὐ λανθάνει διὰ τὰ αὐτά: οὐ διεξοδεύουσα δὲ τὸ πόρρω τοῦ διαστήματος οἷόν ἐστι κατ’ εἶδος οὐκ ἂν δύναιτο οὐδ’ ὅσον ἐστὶ κατὰ μέγεθος εἰπεῖν.

flags.taylor: It was the detail that prevented a near object deceiving
flags.why: The Greek says only that "how great the near is does not escape us, for the same reasons" (διὰ τὰ αὐτά): seeing the forms of its parts.

paragraphs.modern: That things look smaller because the angles of sight are smaller has been said elsewhere not to be so; and now this must be said: whoever says that a thing looks smaller under a smaller angle leaves the sight seeing something outside it, or something else outside altogether, such as air. When, then, it leaves nothing, because the mountain is large, but either the mountain is equal to the sight and the sight can no longer see anything else, its extent fitting what is seen, or what is seen even stretches beyond the sight's reach on either side, what would one say here, when the thing looks much smaller than it is, and yet is seen with the whole sight? And if one looked at the heaven, one would learn it beyond dispute. For no one could see the whole hemisphere with one glance, nor could the sight be poured out so far, stretching up to it. But if anyone wishes, let it be granted. If, then, the whole sight took in the whole, and the size of the heaven is many times that of what appears, how could one make the lessening of the angle the cause of its looking much less than it is?
paragraphs.greek: τὸ δὲ κατὰ τὰς τῆς ὄψεως γωνίας ἐλάττους εἴρηται μὲν καὶ ἐν ἄλλοις ὡς οὐκ ἔστι, καὶ νῦν δὲ ἐκεῖνο λεκτέον, ὡς ὁ λέγων ἔλαττον φαίνεσθαι ἐλάττονι γωνίᾳ καταλείπει τὴν ὄψιν ἔξωθέν τι ὁρῶσαν ἢ ἄλλο τι ὂν ἔξωθεν ὅλως, οἷον ἀέρα. ὅταν οὖν μηδὲν καταλείπῃ τῷ πολὺ εἶναι τὸ ὄρος, ἀλλ’ ἢ ἰσάζῃ καὶ μηκέτι ἄλλο οἷόν τε ᾖ αὐτῇ ὁρᾶν, ἅτε τοῦ διαστήματος αὐτῆς συναρμόσαντος τῷ ὁρωμένῳ, ἢ καὶ ὑπερτείνῃ τὸ ὁρώμενον ἐφ̓ ἑκάτερα τὴν τῆς ὄφεως προσβολήν, τί ἄν τις ἐνταῦθα λέγοι ἐλάττονος μὲν ἢ ἔστι πολλῷ φαινομένου τοῦ ὑποκειμένου, πάσῃ δὲ τῇ ὄψει ὁρωμένου; εἰ δὲ δὴ καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ θεωροῖ, ἀναμφισβητήτως μάθοι ἄν τις. πᾶν μὲν γὰρ τὸ ἡμισφαίριον οὐκ ἄν τις ὁρᾶν μιᾷ προσβολῇ δύναιτο, οὐδὲ ἐπὶ τοσοῦτον χυθῆναι ἡ ὄψις μέχρις αὐτοῦ ἐκτεινομένη. ἀλλ’ εἴ τις βούλεται, δεδόσθω. εἰ οὖν πᾶσα μὲν περιέλαβε πᾶν, πολλαπλάσιον δὲ τὸ μέγεθος τοῦ φαινομένου ὑπάρχει ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ, τοῦ ἔλαττον πολλῷ ἢ ἔστι φαίνεσθαι πῶς ἂν ἐλάττωσιν γωνίας αἰτιῷτο;

flags.taylor: No part of the eye is unoccupied
flags.why: The Greek speaks of the sight (ἡ ὄψις) that the mountain leaves nothing of, not the eye.

flags.taylor: the eye directed to it could not cover so vast an expanse
flags.why: The Greek says the sight could not "be poured out" (χυθῆναι) so far, "stretching up to it": sight goes out from the eye, as in Plato's Timaeus.

notes: The angle of sight is the geometers' account: in Euclid's Optics (definitions 1-4) sight goes out from the eye in straight rays that make a cone, and things seen under a greater angle look greater. The ray of sight going out from the eye is also Plato's (Timaeus 45b-d). Which treatise "elsewhere" means is not known.

paragraphs.modern: Everything that comes to be, and everything that is, either comes to be and is through a cause, or both are without a cause. Or, in both, some things are without a cause and some with one. Or all that comes to be has a cause, while of the things that are, some have a cause and some do not, or none has. Or, the other way round, all the things that are have a cause, while of the things that come to be, some have one and some do not, or none of them has. Now among eternal things, the first cannot be traced back to other causes, since they are first; but those that hang from the first may have their being from them. And whoever gives the activities of each should trace them back to their substances: for this is their being, to give out such an activity.
paragraphs.greek: Ἅπαντα τὰ γινόμενα καὶ τὰ ὄντα ἤτοι κατ’ αἰτίας γίνεται καὶ ἔστι, ἢ ἄνευ αἰτίας ἄμφω: ἢ τὰ μὲν ἄνευ αἰτίας, τὰ δὲ μετ’ αἰτίας ἐν ἀμφοτέροις: ἢ τὰ μὲν γιγνόμενα μετ’ αἰτίας πάντα, τὰ δὲ ὄντα τὰ μέν ἐστιν αὐτῶν μετ’ αἰτίας, τὰ δὲ ἄνευ αἰτίας, ἢ οὐδὲν μετ’ αἰτίας: ἢ ἀνάπαλιν τὰ μὲν ὄντα μετ’ αἰτίας πάντα, τὰ δὲ γιγνόμενα τὰ μὲν οὕτως, τὰ δὲ ἐκείνως, ἢ οὐδὲν αὐτῶν μετ’ αἰτίας. ἐπὶ μὲν οὖν τῶν ἀιδίων τὰ μὲν πρῶτα εἰς ἄλλα αἴτια ἀνάγειν οὐχ οἷόν τε πρῶτα ὄντα: ὅσα δὲ ἐκ τῶν πρώτων ἤρτηται, ἐξ ἐκείνων τὸ εἶναι ἐχέτω. τάς τε ἐνεργείας ἑκάστων ἀποδιδούς τις ἐπὶ τὰς οὐσίας ἀναγέτω: τοῦτο γάρ ἐστι τὸ εἶναι αὐτῶν, τὸ τοιάνδε ἐνέργειαν ἀποδιδόναι.

paragraphs.modern: As for things that come to be, or things that always are but do not always have the same activity, we must say that all of them come to be through causes. What has no cause is not to be admitted. We must give no room to empty swerves, nor to a sudden movement of bodies that arose with nothing going before it, nor to a senseless impulse of a soul, with nothing moving it to do something it did not do before. By this very thing a greater necessity would hold the soul: that it would not be its own, but would be carried by such movements, unwilled and without cause. For either something willed moved it, outside it or inside, or something desired; or, if nothing it reached for moved it, it would not have moved at all.
paragraphs.greek: περὶ δὲ τῶν γιγνομένων ἢ ὄντων μὲν ἀεί, οὐ τὴν αὐτὴν δὲ ἐνέργειαν ποιουμένων ἀεὶ κατ’ αἰτίας ἅπαντα λεκτέον γίνεσθαι, τὸ δὲ ἀναίτιον οὐ παραδεκτέον, οὔτε παρεγκλίσεσι κεναῖς χώραν διδόντα οὔτε κινήσει σωμάτων τῇ ἐξαίφνης, ἣ οὐδενὸς προηγησαμένου ὑπέστη, οὔτε ψυχῆς ὁρμῇ ἐμπλήκτῳ μηδενὸς κινήσαντος αὐτὴν εἰς τό τι πρᾶξαι ὧν πρότερον οὐκ ἐποίει. ἢ αὐτῷ γε τούτῳ μείζων ἄν τις ἔχοι αὐτὴν ἀνάγκη τῷ μὴ αὑτῆς εἶναι, φέρεσθαι δὲ τὰς τοιαύτας φορὰς ἀβουλήτους τε καὶ ἀναιτίους οὔσας. ἢ γὰρ τὸ βουλητόν — τοῦτο δὲ ἢ ἔξω ἢ εἴσω — ἢ τὸ ἐπιθυμητὸν ἐκίνησεν: ἤ, εἰ μηδὲν ὀρεκτὸν ἐκίνησεν, οὐδ’ ἂν ὅλως ἐκινήθη.

flags.taylor: we can make no place here for unwarranted
flags.why: The Greek says "empty swerves" (παρεγκλίσεσι κεναῖς): the swerve of Epicurus' atoms, named by its own word; MacKenna's "unwarranted slantings" hides whose doctrine is meant.

notes: The swerve (παρέγκλισις, Lucretius' clinamen, On the nature of things II.216-293) is the small motion without cause by which Epicurus let atoms meet and left room for free will. Both Plotinus and the Stoics reject motion without a cause (Cicero, On fate 18-25).

paragraphs.modern: Since everything comes to be through causes, it is easy to grasp the near causes of each thing and trace it back to them. For going to the market, say: thinking one must see someone or collect a debt, and in general choosing this or that and setting out for it, and then its seeming right to each to do this. Some things can be traced back to the crafts: the cause of getting well is medicine and the doctor. Of getting rich, a treasure found, or a gift from someone, or making money from labour or a craft. Of a child, the father, and any other help towards begetting that came from outside, one thing from one place and another from another: such and such foods, say, or, a little further off, seed that flows well for begetting, or a wife fit for bearing. And in general, we trace things back to nature.
paragraphs.greek: γιγνομένων δὲ πάντων κατ’ αἰτίας τὰς μὲν προσεχεῖς ἑκάστῳ ῥᾴδιον λαβεῖν καὶ εἰς ταύτας ἀνάγειν: οἷον τοῦ βαδίσαι εἰς ἀγορὰν τὸ οἰηθῆναι δεῖν τινα ἰδεῖν ἢ χρέος ἀπολαβεῖν καὶ ὅλως τὸ τάδε ἢ τάδε ἑλέσθαι καὶ ὁρμῆσαι, ἔπειτα δὲ τὸ φανῆναι ἑκάστῳ ταδὶ ποιεῖν. καὶ τὰ μὲν ἐπὶ τὰς τέχνας ἀνάγειν ἔστιν, οἷον τοῦ ὑγιάσαι αἰτία ἡ ἰατρικὴ καὶ ὁ ἰατρός. καὶ τοῦ πλουτῆσαι θησαυρὸς εὑρεθεὶς ἢ δόσις παρά του ἢ ἐκ πόνων ἢ τέχνης χρηματίσασθαι, καὶ τοῦ τέκνου ὁ πατὴρ καὶ εἴ τι συνεργὸν ἔξωθεν εἰς παιδοποιίαν ἄλλο παῤ ἄλλου ἧκον. οἷον σιτία τοιάδε ἢ καὶ ὀλίγῳ προσώτερα εὔροια εἰς παιδοποιίαν ἢ γυνὴ ἐπιτήδειος εἰς τόκους. καὶ ὅλως εἰς φύσιν.

flags.taylor: by manual or intellectual labour
flags.why: The Greek says "from labours or a craft" (ἐκ πόνων ἢ τέχνης); "intellectual" is MacKenna's.

flags.taylor: or, more immediately, a special organic aptitude
flags.why: The Greek says "a little further off" (ὀλίγῳ προσώτερα), not more immediately, and names "a good flow towards begetting" (εὔροια εἰς παιδοποιίαν), not an aptitude of the organs.

paragraphs.modern: To come this far and stop, and not want to go higher, is perhaps the mark of a lazy man, one who does not listen to those who climb to the first causes and to the causes beyond. For why, when the same things happen, when the moon shines, say, does one man steal and another not? And when like things come from the surrounding air, why does one fall ill and another not? And why is one rich and another poor from the same work? Ways of life, characters and fortunes that differ call on us to go further back. And so, never standing still, some set down bodily principles, such as atoms: by their motion, their blows and their tangling with one another, they make each thing be and come to be as it is, as those atoms are put together and act and are acted on; and our impulses and dispositions too, they say, are as the atoms make them. So they bring this necessity, the one that comes from the atoms, into the things that are. And if someone gives other bodies as principles, and has everything come from them, he makes the things that are slaves to the necessity that comes from those bodies.
paragraphs.greek: μέχρι μὲν οὖν τούτων ἐλθόντα ἀναπαύσασθαι καὶ πρὸς τὸ ἄνω μὴ ἐθελῆσαι χωρεῖν ῥᾳθύμου ἴσως καὶ οὐ κατακούοντος τῶν ἐπὶ τὰ πρῶτα καὶ ἐπὶ τὰ ἐπέκεινα αἴτια ἀνιόντων. διὰ τί γὰρ τῶν αὐτῶν γενομένων, οἷον τῆς σελήνης φανείσης, ὁ μὲν ἥρπασεν, ὁ δὲ οὔ; καὶ τῶν ὁμοίων ἐκ τοῦ περιέχοντος ἡκόντων ὁ μὲν ἐνόσησεν, ὁ δὲ οὔ; καὶ ὁ μὲν πλούσιος, ὁ δὲ πένης ἐκ τῶν αὐτῶν ἔργων. καὶ τρόποι δὴ καὶ ἤθη διάφορα καὶ τύχαι ἐπὶ τὰ πόρρω ἀξιοῦσιν ἰέναι: καὶ οὕτω δὴ ἀεὶ οὐχ ἱστάμενοι οἱ μὲν ἀρχὰς σωματικὰς θέμενοι, οἷον ἀτόμους, τῇ τούτων φορᾷ καὶ πληγαῖς καὶ συμπλοκαῖς πρὸς ἄλληλα ἕκαστα ποιοῦντες καὶ οὕτως ἔχειν καὶ γίνεσθαι, ᾗ ἐκεῖνα συνέστη ποιεῖ τε καὶ πάσχει, καὶ τὰς ἡμετέρας ὁρμὰς καὶ διαθέσεις ταύτῃ ἔχειν, ὡς ἂν ἐκεῖναι ποιῶσιν, ἀνάγκην ταύτην καὶ τὴν παρὰ τούτων εἰς τὰ ὄντα εἰσάγουσι. κἂν ἄλλα δέ τις σώματα ἀρχὰς διδῷ καὶ ἐκ τούτων τὰ πάντα γίγνεσθαι, τῇ παρὰ τούτων ἀνάγκῃ δουλεύειν ποιεῖ τὰ ὄντα.

flags.taylor: even upon Real Being
flags.why: The Greek says only "into the things that are" (εἰς τὰ ὄντα), the things of this world; MacKenna's capitals make it the intelligible world.

paragraphs.modern: Others go up to the principle of the universe and bring everything down from it. They say a cause runs through all things, and that it not only moves each thing but makes it; they set it down as destiny, and as the most sovereign cause. And not only all else that comes to be, but our own thoughts too, they say, come from its movements, as the parts of an animal each move not from themselves but from the ruling part in each animal. Others say that the revolution of the universe holds all things and makes all things by its motion, and by the relations and figures of the planets and the fixed stars towards one another; trusting in the foretelling that comes from these, they hold that each thing comes to be from there.
paragraphs.greek: οἱ δὲ ἐπὶ τὴν τοῦ παντὸς ἀρχὴν ἐλθόντες ἀπ’ αὐτῆς κατάγουσι πάντα, διὰ πάντων φοιτήσασαν αἰτίαν καὶ ταύτην οὐ μόνον κινοῦσαν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ποιοῦσαν ἕκαστα λέγοντες, εἱμαρμένην ταύτην καὶ κυριωτάτην αἰτίαν θέμενοι αὐτὴν οὖσαν, καὶ πάντα οὐ μόνον τὰ ἄλλα, ὅσα γίνεται, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰς ἡμετέρας διανοήσεις ἐκ τῶν ἐκείνης ἰέναι κινημάτων, οἷον ζῴου μορίων κινουμένων ἑκάστων οὐκ ἐξ ἑαυτῶν, ἐκ δὲ τοῦ ἡγεμονοῦντος ἐν ἑκάστῳ τῶν ζῴων. ἄλλοι δὲ τὴν τοῦ παντὸς φορὰν περιέχουσαν καὶ πάντα ποιοῦσαν τῇ κινήσει καὶ ταῖς τῶν ἄστρων πλανωμένων τε καὶ ἀπλανῶν σχέσεσι καὶ σχηματισμοῖς πρὸς ἄλληλα, ἀπὸ τῆς ἐκ τούτων προρρήσεως πιστούμενοι, ἕκαστα ἐντεῦθεν γίνεσθαι ἀξιοῦσι.

flags.taylor: the leading principle which animal life presupposes
flags.why: The Greek says "the ruling part in each animal" (τοῦ ἡγεμονοῦντος ἐν ἑκάστῳ τῶν ζῴων), the Stoics' word for the commanding part of the soul; "which animal life presupposes" is MacKenna's.

notes: The Stoics called destiny (εἱμαρμένη) a cause running through all things, the reason of the cosmos (Chrysippus in Stobaeus, Eclogues I.79; Cicero, On divination I.125-126), and the ruling part (ἡγεμονικόν) the part of the soul that moves the rest, as a spider in the middle of its web.

paragraphs.modern: And if someone speaks of the weaving together of causes with one another, and of the chain from above, the later things always following the earlier and going back to them, since they came to be through them and would not have come to be without them, and the later being slaves to what is before them, he will plainly be bringing in destiny in another way. One would not miss the truth if he set these too down as two kinds: for some hang everything from some one thing, and others do not. We shall speak about these. But now the argument must go to the first; then, in order, we must look at the others.
paragraphs.greek: καὶ μὴν καὶ τὴν τῶν αἰτίων ἐπιπλοκὴν πρὸς ἄλληλα καὶ τὸν ἄνωθεν εἱρμὸν καὶ τὸ ἕπεσθαι τοῖς προτέροις ἀεὶ τὰ ὕστερα καὶ ταῦτα ἐπ’ ἐκεῖνα ἀνιέναι δἰ αὐτῶν γενόμενα καὶ ἄνευ ἐκείνων οὐκ ἂν γενόμενα δουλεύειν τε τοῖς πρὸ αὐτῶν τὰ ὕστερα, ταῦτα εἴ τις λέγοι, εἱμαρμένην ἕτερον τρόπον εἰσάγων φανεῖται. διττοὺς δὲ ἄν τις θέμενος καὶ τούτους οὐκ ἂν τοῦ ἀληθοῦς ἀποτυγχάνοι. οἱ μὲν γὰρ ἀφ̓ ἑνός τινος τὰ πάντα ἀναρτῶσιν, οἱ δὲ οὐχ οὕτως. λεχθήσεται δὲ περὶ τούτων. νῦν δὲ ἐπὶ τοὺς πρώτους ἰτέον τῷ λόγῳ: εἶτ̓ ἐφεξῆς τὰ τῶν ἄλλων ἐπισκεπτέον.

flags.taylor: Of this last opinion we will have something to say
flags.why: The Greek says "we shall speak about these" (λεχθήσεται δὲ περὶ τούτων), "but now we must go to the first" (ἐπὶ τοὺς πρώτους), "then look at the others in order": the first named, the atoms, are taken first, in chapter 3.

notes: "The chain" (εἱρμός) is the Stoic word: destiny, they said, is the chain of causes (Aetius I.28.4; Cicero, On fate 20).

paragraphs.modern: To hand all things over to bodies, whether atoms or what are called elements, and to have their disorderly motion beget order, reason and the soul that leads, is absurd and impossible both ways; but more impossible, if one can say so, is the one from atoms. Many true arguments have been given about these. But even if someone did set down such principles, it would not follow of necessity, either, that there is necessity over all things, or destiny in some other way. Suppose, first, that there are atoms. They will move, some downwards (let there be a down), others sideways, as it happens, each one differently. Nothing, then, will be in order, since there is no order; and what comes to be, once it has come to be, will simply be. So there would be no foretelling or prophecy at all, neither by a craft (for how could there be a craft of things without order?), nor by inspiration and possession by a god: for here too what is to be must be fixed.
paragraphs.greek: σώμασι μὲν οὖν ἐπιτρέψαι τὰ πάντα εἴτε ἀτόμοις εἴτε τοῖς στοιχείοις καλουμένοις καὶ τῇ ἐκ τούτων ἀτάκτῳ φορᾷ τάξιν καὶ λόγον καὶ ψυχὴν τὴν ἡγουμένην γεννᾶν ἀμφοτέρως μὲν ἄτοπον καὶ ἀδύνατον, ἀδυνατώτερον δέ, εἰ οἷόν τε λέγειν, τὸ ἐξ ἀτόμων. καὶ περὶ τούτων πολλοὶ εἴρηνται λόγοι ἀληθεῖς. εἰ δὲ δὴ καὶ θεῖτό τις τοιαύτας ἀρχάς, οὐδ’ οὕτως ἀναγκαῖον οὔτε τὴν κατὰ πάντων ἀνάγκην οὔτε τὴν ἄλλως εἱμαρμένην ἕπεσθαι. φέρε γὰρ πρῶτον τὰς ἀτόμους εἶναι. αὗται τοίνυν κινήσονται τὴν μὲν εἰς τὸ κάτω — ἔστω γάρ τι κάτω — τὴν δ’ ἐκ πλαγίων, ὅπῃ ἔτυχεν, ἄλλαι κατὰ ἄλλα. οὐδὲν δὴ τακτῶς, τάξεώς γε οὐκ οὔσης, τὸ δὲ γενόμενον τοῦτο, ὅτε γέγονε, πάντως. ὥστε οὔτε πρόρρησις οὔτε μαντικὴ τὸ παράπαν ἂν εἴη, οὔτε εἴ τις ἐκ τέχνης — πῶς γὰρ ἐπὶ τοῖς ἀτάκτοις τέχνη; — οὔτε εἴ τις ἐξ ἐνθουσιασμοῦ καὶ ἐπιπνοίας: δεῖ γὰρ καὶ ἐνταῦθα ὡρισμένον τὸ μέλλον εἶναι.

flags.taylor: A good deal of truth has resulted
flags.why: The Greek says "many true arguments have been given about these" (πολλοὶ εἴρηνται λόγοι ἀληθεῖς), that is, against the atoms; MacKenna makes the theory itself yield truth.

flags.taylor: admitting a down and an up
flags.why: The Greek has only "let there be a down" (ἔστω γάρ τι κάτω); the "up", and MacKenna's words in brackets on the universe, are his.

flags.taylor: this Universe, when it achieves existence, is all order
flags.why: The Greek says "what has come to be, when it has come to be, is wholly so" (τὸ δὲ γενόμενον τοῦτο, ὅτε γέγονε, πάντως): it is settled only after the event, which is why nothing can be foretold. Nothing is said of the universe or of order.

paragraphs.modern: Bodies, struck by the atoms, will have to suffer of necessity whatever the atoms bring. But to what motions of atoms will anyone trace the works and experiences of the soul?
